passages.text: The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE, was the largest state the world had seen, reaching from the Balkans and Egypt to the Indus. Its kings ruled dozens of peoples through satraps, roads and a common administrative language, and mostly let them keep their gods and laws.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Royal Road ran about 2,700 kilometers from Susa to Sardis; Herodotus says a traveler took ninety days and a relay of royal couriers about a week.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Qanats, tunnels that carry groundwater out to the plains, spread across Iran under the empire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Darius I struck the gold daric and the silver siglos, the first coins used across the whole empire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Darius began Persepolis, with its terrace, hundred-columned halls, bull capitals and staircases carved with tribute-bearers from every province.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay text from Babylon, records Cyrus restoring temples and sending deported peoples home; the modern description of it as a charter of human rights is disputed by historians.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The kings invoked Ahura Mazda in their inscriptions; how far the court followed Zoroaster's teaching is debated.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Cyrus let the Judean exiles in Babylon return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple, as the Hebrew Bible records.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Some twenty satrapies paid tribute in silver and kind, each under a governor watched by the king's inspectors.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Roads, coinage and a long peace tied the Mediterranean to Central Asia and India.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imperial Aramaic served as the language of administration from Egypt to Bactria.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Iranian dynasties, the Sasanians above all, looked back to the Achaemenids.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Alexander and the Seleucids kept the satrapies and much of the administration.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Persepolis was listed by UNESCO.
Alexander defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BCE and burned Persepolis in 330. Darius was killed by his own satrap the same year, and Alexander took the empire as its heir.

passages.text: Aksum linked the northern Ethiopian highlands to the Red Sea through Adulis. Its monuments and inscriptions reveal a kingdom connected to African and Mediterranean exchange networks. The city also retained religious and ceremonial importance after its political power diminished.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Stoneworkers carved enormous stelae from single blocks. Some imitate multi-storey buildings, preserving an architectural vocabulary in stone.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The carved stelae belong especially to the third and fourth centuries CE. Royal tombs and later palace ruins reveal several phases of monumental construction.

passages.title: Writing and ideas
passages.text: King Ezana's fourth-century inscriptions used Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez. Their multiple languages make connections across the region visible.

passages.title: Writing and ideas
passages.text: Christianity was introduced during the fourth century. Church building subsequently became part of the city's sacred landscape.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Adulis connected maritime commerce with inland routes, while ivory trade linked Aksum with Sudan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Ethiopian emperors continued to be crowned at Aksum. Political decline did not erase its ceremonial role.

passages.text: The Almohads made Marrakesh a center of government and learning while maintaining a major Iberian center at Seville. Monumental mosques, gates and city walls gave their rule an enduring architectural presence.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Kutubiyya mosque and minaret formed a major landmark in Marrakesh. Walls and monumental gateways also shaped the imperial capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Almohad decoration emphasized organized geometric patterns and increasingly schematic ornament.

passages.title: Ideas and learning
passages.text: The courts at Marrakesh and Seville supported Islamic learning within a program of religious reform.

passages.title: Urban life
passages.text: Fez expanded under the Almohads, with the old city reaching the extent described by UNESCO as its present-day size.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Almohad Marrakesh remained a capital into the thirteenth century. Later dynasties inherited a city whose monuments continued to structure urban life.

passages.text: The Almoravids governed from Marrakesh and connected Saharan routes with North African and Iberian towns. Their rule supported major religious buildings and crafts, while their capital helped shape the urban geography of the western Islamic world.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Marrakesh was an Almoravid foundation. Its palm grove is traditionally attributed to their period, linking the capital with a managed cultivated landscape.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ali ibn Yusuf commissioned a richly worked mosque minbar in 1137. It later became associated with the Kutubiyya Mosque.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Textile manufacture in Almeria shows that Almoravid cultural production included luxurious fabrics as well as mosque building.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Almoravid power connected important ports with trans-Saharan commerce. The state's economy crossed both sea and desert.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Almohads replaced Almoravid rule in Marrakesh in the mid-twelfth century and retained the city as a capital.

passages.text: Asante architecture joined construction skill with visual language and religious practice. Surviving shrine buildings near Kumasi preserve parts of a tradition that remained meaningful beyond the period of imperial power.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders arranged timber and bamboo structures around courtyards, applying mud plaster to walls and originally roofing them with thatch.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall reliefs combine spirals with animal, bird and plant forms. Motifs related to Adinkra convey meanings as well as decorate surfaces.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shrines are places for consultation with deities before important decisions. Their symbolic features belong to continuing religious practice.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maintaining earthen buildings requires responding to heavy rain, humidity and damage to organic materials. Architectural survival depends on repeated care.

passages.text: Ayutthaya, founded on an island in the Chao Phraya in 1351, ruled Siam for four centuries and was one of the great trading cities of Asia. Its kings took the Khmer idea of divine kingship, and its port welcomed Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Dutch, Portuguese and French merchants.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rice, deer hides, sappanwood and tin left through the royal warehouses; Chinese junks and, from 1511, Portuguese ships came to buy them.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Foreign quarters ringed the city: Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch from 1608, French and Persian; the Greek Constantine Phaulkon rose to chief minister under King Narai.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Narai sent an embassy to Louis XIV at Versailles in 1686.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Prang towers in the Khmer manner and the tall chedis of Wat Phra Si Sanphet, with gilded Buddhas.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Court poetry, the Ramakien, the Thai Ramayana, and masked dance drama.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism with royal patronage and hundreds of temples in the capital.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Khmer court ritual and the devaraja idea of the king as a god shaped kingship; the law code of 1805 preserves Ayutthaya's laws.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic City of Ayutthaya was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Thai kingship, law and court culture descend from Ayutthaya.
A Burmese army took and burned the city in April 1767. Within the year Taksin had rallied Siam from a new capital at Thonburi.

passages.text: Tenochtitlan brought canals, markets, workshops and ceremonial architecture into a large lake city. This card focuses on the capital's civic and artistic life within the Aztec imperial world.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and raised causeways connected the capital to surrounding lakeshore towns. Canoes carried people and goods through the urban network.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Aqueducts supplied fresh water, while neighborhood communities maintained local temples and markets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stone carvers used stone and hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand to shape even hard materials into detailed sculpture.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The Templo Mayor paired shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. Successive rulers enlarged the complex, sometimes also responding to flooding and unstable ground.

passages.title: Craft and exchange
passages.text: The capital's markets offered food and luxury goods. Its neighborhoods included potters, weavers, sculptors, lapidaries and featherworkers.
Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Spanish rulers built a new colonial capital over the devastated city.

passages.text: Baekje held the southwest of the Korean peninsula and was the most refined of the Three Kingdoms, trading by sea with China and Japan. Its monks, scholars and craftsmen carried Buddhism, Chinese learning and temple architecture to the Yamato court.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Sea routes linked Baekje to the southern Chinese dynasties and to Japan, and possibly further south.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Seong sent a Buddha image, sutras and monks to the Yamato court, the official introduction of Buddhism to Japan; Japanese sources date it to 538 or 552.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Baekje smile, the gentle expression of its stone and bronze Buddhas, as on the rock-cut triad at Seosan.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze Buddhas, reliquaries and roof tiles stamped with lotus designs.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Gilt-bronze Incense Burner of Baekje, found at Neungsan-ri in 1993, a mountain of peaks, musicians and animals on a lotus base.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Marananta arrived from Eastern Jin and the court adopted Buddhism, building temples and monastic communities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning and the Chinese classics were taught to the aristocracy; Baekje scholars such as Wang In took the classics to Japan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Baekje Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Baekje's transmission of Buddhism, writing and craft shaped early Japanese civilization.
A Silla army and a Tang fleet took the capital Sabi in 660; a restoration movement was crushed at the Baekgang river in 663, and Silla absorbed the land by 676.

passages.text: Balhae was founded in 698 by Dae Joyeong, a former Goguryeo general, in the hills of eastern Manchuria, and grew into a power that Tang writers called the Flourishing State of the East. Its capitals were laid out on the Tang model and its envoys sailed regularly to Japan.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Embassies went to Tang China and, more than thirty times, across the sea to Japan, carrying furs, ginseng and horses.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Balhae sat on the routes between Manchuria, the Korean peninsula, north China and the steppe.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism was practiced in the capitals, alongside the native beliefs of the Mohe majority.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A Tang-style government of three chancelleries and six ministries ran a state of many peoples; the capital Sanggyeong copied the grid of Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Korea, China and Russia each claim Balhae's story in their national histories.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Excavations of its walled capitals and tombs show a state that mixed Goguryeo, Mohe and Tang traditions.
The Khitan under Yelü Abaoji, founder of what became the Liao dynasty, took the capital Sanggyeong in 926 after a campaign of a few weeks. Refugees from the ruling class moved south into Goryeo.

passages.text: Benin's court commissioned brass sculpture to preserve royal memory and express authority. This Edo kingdom was centered in present-day Nigeria, distinct from the modern country named Benin.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: An incoming oba commissioned a commemorative head honoring his predecessor. These idealized royal images emphasize kingship rather than individual facial likeness.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Brass-casting guild artists produced rectangular plaques for the palace. A surviving example is dated approximately 1540 to 1570.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Palace courtyards and galleries included wooden pillars covered with cast brass plaques.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Scholars interpret palace plaques as an archive later consulted about court ritual and regalia.

passages.title: Historical evidence
passages.text: British removal of royal works in 1897 disrupted their original contexts. Scholars therefore combine stylistic and material evidence when reconstructing their chronology.

passages.text: Cao Wei was the most powerful of the Three Kingdoms, controlling the northern heartland of China. Founded by Cao Cao's son Cao Pi, it inherited the Han administrative system and produced significant literary and military achievements.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cao Cao and his sons Cao Pi and Cao Zhi wrote some of the finest poetry of the age, the Jian'an style named for the last Han reign period.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cao Pi's Discourse on Literature, the first systematic essay of Chinese literary criticism, argues that writing outlasts rank and wealth.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ma Jun builds a south-pointing chariot, a cart whose figure keeps pointing south as it turns, through gearing whose design is reconstructed with differential gears.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The tuntian system of military-agricultural colonies, begun by Cao Cao in 196 under the last Han emperor, settled soldiers and refugees on frontier land.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Administrative innovations passed to the Jin dynasty, among them the nine-rank system for grading officials, introduced in 220.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The fourteenth-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms later romanticized this era.
Sima Yan forced the last Wei emperor to abdicate and founded the Jin dynasty, in the last month of 265 by the Chinese calendar, February 266 by ours.

passages.text: Carolingian rulers made learning, Christian worship and patronage part of imperial government. Their workshops and scholars adapted older traditions into books, buildings and objects that influenced medieval Europe.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: The drive for accurate, readable texts encouraged Carolingian minuscule, a clear script based on Roman letter forms.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Charlemagne gathered scholars including Alcuin, Theodulf and Paul the Lombard. Court patronage supported educational and liturgical reform.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Illuminated books and carved ivory panels combined classical figures with local ornamental traditions. Precious bindings could include gems and pearls.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The palace chapel at Aachen has an octagonal core, an encircling aisle, upper galleries and a dome. Its antique columns were probably brought from Rome and Ravenna.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: Charlemagne received the imperial crown in Rome in 800. The ceremony tied royal authority to a Christian interpretation of Roman imperial tradition.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Carolingian art continued after Charlemagne's death and political fragmentation. The end of a unified realm did not end its workshops or manuscript traditions.

passages.text: Carthage grew on the Gulf of Tunis into a major center of Punic civilization and Mediterranean commerce. Its ports connected communities, goods and artistic traditions. This card concerns the Punic city and its power before Roman destruction, rather than the later Roman city built on the same site.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The surviving Punic harbor remains make maritime infrastructure central to understanding Carthage's commercial power.

passages.title: Arts and beliefs
passages.text: Stelae from the sacred tophet show varied cultural influences. The imagery is evidence of artistic exchange as well as religious practice.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Magon was remembered as an agronomist and Hannon as a navigator. Agriculture and seafaring both belonged to Carthage's intellectual legacy.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Roman buildings at Carthage belong to a refounded city. They should not be attributed automatically to Punic builders.
Rome destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE. A Roman city was later established on the site.

passages.text: Champa was a string of Cham kingdoms along the coast of what is now central Vietnam, first recorded by the Chinese as Lin-yi in 192 CE. Seafarers and traders, the Chams built brick towers to Shiva and fought the Khmer and the Vietnamese for more than a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Brick tower temples at My Son, built from the seventh to the thirteenth century, with sandstone carving of a fineness that rivals Angkor.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sandstone images of Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha and dancing apsaras in the Cham styles of Tra Kieu and Dong Duong.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham ports sold agarwood, ivory, gold and cinnamon to China and the archipelago and sheltered ships waiting for the monsoon.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham sailors traded and raided across the South China Sea and up the Mekong; they sacked Angkor in 1177.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shaivism was the royal cult, with Buddhism strong at Dong Duong in the ninth century; Islam reached the Chams from the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions record kings and gifts to temples; the Dong Yen Chau stone of the fourth century is the oldest text in any Southeast Asian language.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: My Son Sanctuary was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Cham communities in Vietnam and Cambodia keep the language and, in Cambodia, Islam.
The Vietnamese took the capital Vijaya in 1471; the last Cham principality, Panduranga, was absorbed by the Nguyen emperor Minh Mang in 1832.

passages.text: The Chimu kingdom made Chan Chan a major center on Peru's north coast. Its earthen compounds, craft production and water systems show how a large city organized resources in a dry coastal environment.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and irrigation supported agriculture around Chan Chan. Roads helped connect the kingdom along the northern coast.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Large walled compounds contained open courts, temples, dwellings, storage spaces, reservoirs and funerary platforms.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Earthen walls carried relief decoration with abstract patterns and human or animal subjects.

passages.title: Craft and work
passages.text: Specialized production areas supported weaving, woodworking and metalworking. These activities were part of the city's planned fabric.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Storage and water-management installations supported the city alongside agricultural land beyond its monumental center.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The kingdom reached its height in the fifteenth century before incorporation into the Inca Empire. The source used here does not establish a precise conquest year.

passages.text: The Cholas of the Kaveri delta, restored under Vijayalaya in 848, ruled the Tamil south for four centuries and sent fleets across the Bay of Bengal. Their bronze Natarajas, the great temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram and their village assemblies are the high point of Tamil civilization.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rajaraja I finished the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, its granite tower about 66 meters high.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze images of Shiva Nataraja, cast by the lost-wax method, reached their classic form in the tenth and eleventh centuries.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rajendra I sent a fleet against Srivijaya in 1025 and sacked its ports along the Strait of Malacca.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Merchant guilds such as the Ayyavole Five Hundred traded across the Indian Ocean, and Chola embassies reached Song China in 1015 and 1077.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tanks, sluices and the Kaveri's old anicuts irrigated the delta's rice fields.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ocean-going ships carried armies to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Sumatra.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Village assemblies chose their committees by lot from eligible landholders, as the Uttaramerur inscriptions of the 920s record.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Great Living Chola Temples were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chola bronzes and temple styles were carried to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
The Pandyas of Madurai defeated the Cholas repeatedly from the 1210s and absorbed the last of the kingdom by 1279.

passages.text: Outer, inner and private courtyards structured access through each palace, making social distinctions part of the built environment.

passages.text: Five dynasties of Turkic and Afghan sultans ruled from Delhi from 1206 to 1526, at their height under the Khaljis and Tughluqs reaching the far south. They brought Persian letters, Islamic architecture and Sufi shrines to northern India, and their India shaped the Mughals.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Qutb Minar was begun under Qutb al-Din Aibak and finished by Iltutmish; at 72.5 meters it is the tallest brick minaret in the world.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The true arch and dome arrived with the sultanate; the Alai Darwaza of 1311 is the first building in India built entirely on those principles.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Amir Khusrau of Delhi wrote Persian verse and is credited with the beginnings of Hindustani music and poetry.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Chishti Sufis such as Nizamuddin Auliya drew Hindus and Muslims alike to their shrines and their music.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Persian was the language of court and chancery, and Indo-Persian history writing began with Minhaj-i Siraj and Barani.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Alauddin Khalji fixed market prices and had the land measured for revenue; paper and the spinning wheel spread through India in these centuries.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Persian wheels lifted water for irrigation.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Indo-Islamic culture and the Persian chancery passed to the Mughals.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Qutb Minar and its monuments were listed by UNESCO.
Babur's guns and cavalry defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in April 1526, and the Mughal Empire began.

passages.text: Twentieth-century Copenhagen became a meeting place for physicists working on quantum theory. This focused chapter follows the institute, discussions and everyday arrangements that helped international collaboration take root.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics was dedicated in Copenhagen in March 1921, after fundraising and approval of the project.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: During the 1920s, visiting researchers exchanged ideas in Copenhagen. Discussions could happen in small groups and at dinners with the Bohr family.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: In 1927, Bohr presented complementarity: different experimental arrangements can require different, mutually exclusive descriptions of a quantum phenomenon. The proposal became a focus of debate.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the 1930s, a new mathematics institute was built beside the physics institute. Shared classrooms and a canteen were intended to support closer collaboration.

passages.text: This chapter follows sixteenth-century Denmark-Norway through astronomy, printing and royal architecture. Tycho Brahe's observatory shows how scientific work depended on buildings, instruments and supporting crafts.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Under Danish royal patronage, Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg on Hven between 1576 and 1580. The island is now Swedish but was then Danish.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Uraniborg included a printing office and a water mill for making paper. Publishing and material production supported the observatory's work.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Tycho established Stjerneborg in 1584. Sheltered instrument spaces reduced exposure to wind and helped stabilize observations.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Frederik II began rebuilding Kronborg as a Renaissance castle in 1574. Its courtyard, carved sandstone and decorated chapel formed a major royal setting.

passages.text: Eastern Wu controlled the Yangzi delta and southern coast under the Sun family. Its naval power and maritime trade connected China to Southeast Asia, while southern China developed economically and culturally.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Shipbuilding for the Yangzi and the sea: the stern-mounted rudder, attested in Han tomb models, and ships with several masts, described by Wu envoys who sailed to the south.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Maritime trade with Southeast Asia and India; in 226 a merchant from the Roman east named Qin Lun reached the Wu court.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Exotic goods imported from the south: pearls, ivory, rhinoceros horn.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Economic development of the Yangzi delta laid foundations for later southern prosperity.
The Jin dynasty launched a massive invasion with naval forces sailing down the Yangzi, forcing Wu to surrender and reunifying China.

passages.text: The Eastern Zhou saw the Zhou kings reduced to figureheads while rival states competed for power. This political fragmentation paradoxically produced China's greatest intellectual flowering, as philosophers offered competing visions of the good society.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucius born in the state of Lu; he teaches ethics, proper conduct and the restoration of Zhou ritual.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mozi advocates universal love and utilitarian ethics as alternatives to Confucianism.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Daodejing, attributed to the sage Laozi, is in circulation by about 300 BCE, the date of the earliest copies found in a tomb at Guodian; it founds the Daoist philosophy of naturalness and non-action.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mencius develops Confucian ideas of innate human goodness and the right to rebel against unjust rulers.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Cast iron production begins, allowing mass production of agricultural tools.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Crossbows with bronze trigger mechanisms appear in warfare.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron tools replace stone and bronze in agriculture and crafts.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Spring and Autumn Annals compiled in Lu, the first Chinese chronicle history, covering 722 to 481 BCE.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Zuozhuan and other commentaries elaborate on historical events with narrative detail.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Lacquerware production reaches new heights of craftsmanship, above all in the southern state of Chu.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Walled cities grow as commercial centers with specialized crafts and markets.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Coinage in bronze spade and knife shapes facilitates trade between states.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Professional bureaucrats and scholars travel between courts seeking employment.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Trade networks connect the Yellow River states with the Yangzi valley and the southern coast.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Salt and iron become major commodities in interstate commerce.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Hundred Schools of Thought established the major philosophical traditions of East Asia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Military innovations and statecraft from this period influenced later imperial administration.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The concept of a unified Chinese cultural sphere emerged despite political division.
The Qin state conquered the last Zhou territories in 256 BCE, and the last Zhou king died that year, ending the dynasty.

passages.text: Ancient Egypt brought together royal power, skilled workshops and a durable written culture along the Nile. Its art changed substantially across the Old and Middle Kingdoms. Pyramids, family memorials and ordinary letters reveal different parts of that society; surviving evidence is often weighted toward elite tombs.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Saqqara, Djoser's Step Pyramid formed the center of a complex of stone buildings and underground chambers. Later builders developed smooth-sided pyramids.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Papyrus sheets were made by layering strips of the stalk's inner pith and drying them under pressure. Sheets could be joined into writing rolls.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Old Kingdom tomb chapels depicted food offerings and agricultural work. These images were meant to sustain the dead, so they are more than documentary pictures of daily life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Middle Kingdom jewelers placed tiny inlays on ornaments and sometimes decorated their backs with elaborate chasing, visible principally to their wearers.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Unis had religious spells carved inside his pyramid late in Dynasty 5. Later kings, and eventually queens, also received these Pyramid Texts.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Middle Kingdom memorials increasingly pictured extended families and associates. Such monuments show religious commemoration reaching beyond the ruler alone.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Papyrus carried accounts, letters and legal agreements as well as religious works. Black ink usually supplied the main text; red ink could mark emphasis.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The same marsh plant also supplied material for baskets, sandals, ropes and small boats. A writing technology belonged to a much wider craft economy.

passages.text: Elam was one of the oldest civilizations, centered on Susa and the highlands of Anshan in southwestern Iran. Its language belongs to no known family; its kings built ziggurats and fought, traded and intermarried with Mesopotamia for more than two thousand years.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: King Untash-Napirisha built the ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil, the best preserved ziggurat anywhere, with baked-brick stairways and glazed tiles.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Irrigation canals from the Karun and Karkheh rivers watered the Khuzestan plain.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze casting on a large scale: the statue of Queen Napir-Asu from Susa weighs 1,750 kilograms.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Proto-Elamite, one of the earliest scripts, was written on clay at Susa around 3100 BCE and is still undeciphered.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cylinder seals and rock-cut reliefs of kings and processions, as at Kul-e Farah.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A pantheon headed by Inshushinak, the god of Susa, with the goddess Kiririsha and the highland god Napirisha.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Kingship passed between brothers and nephews, and some scholars read the record as descent through the female line, unusual in the ancient Near East.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chogha Zanbil was among the first Iranian sites listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Elamite was one of the three languages of the Achaemenid royal inscriptions, and Elamite scribes kept the Persepolis archives.
Assyria sacked Susa in 647 BCE. The small Elamite kingdoms that followed passed under the Persians of Anshan, and Cyrus's empire, which took Babylon in 539 BCE, made Susa one of its capitals.

passages.text: The medieval Soninke empire of Ghana prospered through trans-Saharan exchange. Its power rested on commercial connections and political centers such as Kumbi Saleh, rather than a fixed border enclosing one people.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold moved north while salt moved south. Taxing imports and exports helped support imperial rule.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Camel caravans made long desert journeys possible; traders connected different ecological regions rather than transporting goods within a single uniform landscape.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Savanna agriculture and livestock breeding supported the societies through which the trade routes passed.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Al-Bakri described gold-adorned court equipment and clothing. Such written testimony records royal display, not the possessions of every household.

passages.title: Political change
passages.text: By the late twelfth century Ghana had lost its dominant position in the western Sudan gold trade as routes shifted. Its decline was a process, not a securely dated disappearance of Soninke society.

passages.text: The Royal Society's first meeting followed Christopher Wren's astronomy lecture in London in 1660. Its members gathered observations, performed experiments and discussed results.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Henry Oldenburg began Philosophical Transactions in 1665. The same year, Robert Hooke published the close observations collected in Micrographia.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The early Royal Society drew members from professional and aristocratic circles and admitted only men. Its meeting rooms represented a restricted part of society.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The English and Scottish Acts of Union created Great Britain on 1 May 1707. The new parliament first met that October.

passages.text: The Etruscans lived in a network of central Italian city-states. Metalworking, imported luxury materials and distinctive funerary art reveal communities deeply involved in Mediterranean exchange.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Bucchero pottery has a glossy black surface and often uses shapes associated with metal vessels.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze workers made decorated chariots, vessels, mirrors and sculpture. Access to copper and iron supported their craft traditions.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Greek painted pottery was highly valued in Etruria. Trade also brought ivory, amber and other materials used by local artists.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: At Cerveteri, rock-cut tombs reproduce features of houses. Their arrangement into streets and small squares offers clues to settlement planning.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Painted tombs at Tarquinia preserve scenes of living, dying and religious belief. Funerary images provide evidence that short surviving inscriptions often cannot supply.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Roman expansion absorbed the Etruscan cities over time. Their culture did not end on the map's current 323 BCE snapshot boundary.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Canal du Midi project used locks, aqueducts, bridges, spillways and tunnels to make an inland water route. UNESCO dates the wider historic works to 1667 through 1694.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The canal's water-supply system drew on the Montagne Noire. The Saint-Ferreol dam was a major engineering component.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: After 1661, Louis XIV enlarged Versailles through work directed first by Le Vau and later by Jules Hardouin-Mansart. Its architecture developed across successive campaigns.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Andre Le Notre organized Versailles' gardens with long axes, planted beds, hedges, water and fountains. The landscape formed part of the royal residence's design.

passages.text: Frankish communities expressed wealth and identity through dress and skilled metalwork. The map's Frankish Kingdom record covers only part of a longer history and should not imply that Frankish culture began in 600.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Women wore belted tunics with a wrap or cloak. Pendants hung from belts, and jewelry included earrings, necklaces and hairpins.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Small paired brooches were common in earlier centuries; large single disk brooches became fashionable in the 600s.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A mid-seventh-century disk brooch combines gold with garnet, colored glass and mother-of-pearl. Small fastening objects could display elaborate material contrasts.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Charlemagne became king of the Franks in 768 and emperor in 800. Imperial culture grew from earlier Frankish traditions of patronage and fine metalwork.

passages.text: Funan, known from the reports of Chinese envoys in the third century, was the first of Southeast Asia's Indian-influenced states, in the Mekong delta. Its port at Oc Eo linked the trade of Rome, India and China.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Oc Eo's canals and warehouses handled goods between the Gulf of Thailand and the Mekong; coins of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius were found there.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Indian beads and seals, Chinese bronze mirrors and local tin amulets came out of the excavations of the 1940s.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Sanskrit inscriptions and images of Vishnu and Shiva show Indian religion at court, with Buddhism beside it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Chinese envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying, who visited about 245, described walled towns, taxes paid in gold and a written script.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A network of canals, one of them nearly 90 kilometers long, drained and linked the delta towns.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Funan set the pattern of the Indianized kingdom that Chenla, the Chams and the Khmer followed.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Oc Eo is among the earliest excavated urban sites in mainland Southeast Asia.
In the sixth century the inland Khmer state the Chinese called Chenla absorbed Funan; by about 550 its kings ruled the delta.

passages.text: In late-sixteenth- and early-seventeenth-century Genoa, mercantile wealth reshaped streets, houses and hospitality. The Rolli palaces reveal how private residences served the republic's public business.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, Genoa developed the Strade Nuove as a coordinated district of streets and aristocratic palaces above the older city.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The palaces adapted to steep and confined sites with open staircases, courtyards and garden-facing loggias. Frescoes and stucco decorated their interiors.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Senate established the Rolli list of private palaces used to lodge distinguished official visitors. Hosting state guests became an obligation attached to selected elite homes.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Rolli system sorted residences into categories corresponding to different ranks of guest. Hospitality made social hierarchy part of the organization of official visits.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Architectural treatises spread knowledge of Genoa's new streets and palaces beyond the city in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

passages.text: Goguryeo was the largest and most martial of Korea's Three Kingdoms, holding the north of the peninsula and much of Manchuria from its mountain fortresses. Its painted tombs are the fullest picture of life in early Korea, and its art reached Japan through Baekje and its own monks.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Tomb murals show hunts, processions, wrestlers, dancers, the sun crow and the moon toad, and the four directional animals, painted with a sense of movement.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze crown ornaments, earrings and belt fittings show skilled metalwork.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist sculpture and temple building grew after the religion arrived in 372; the gilt-bronze Buddha of 539 from Yeonga is the oldest dated Korean Buddhist image.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mountain fortresses of fitted stone, built to the ridgelines, guarded the valleys and river crossings.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron lamellar armor for horse and rider equipped heavy cavalry, as the tomb paintings show.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Sundo arrived from Former Qin with images and sutras, and the court adopted Buddhism; a Confucian academy, the Taehak, was founded the same year.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Native shamanic and ancestral rites continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Complex of Koguryo Tombs in North Korea and the capitals and tombs of the kingdom in China were both listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Korea comes from Goryeo, the tenth-century dynasty that took its name from Goguryeo.

After decades of war with Silla and Tang China, Goguryeo fell when Pyongyang was taken in 668. Tang set up a protectorate over the north; Silla held the peninsula south of the Taedong river and pushed the Tang armies out by 676.

passages.text: The Göktürk Khaganate was the first empire to bear the name Türk. Founded by Bumin in 552, it stretched from Manchuria to the Black Sea, split into eastern and western halves in 583, submitted to Tang in 630 and 657, and rose again as the Second Khaganate in 682. Its stone inscriptions are the oldest Turkic writing.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The stelae of Kül Tegin (732) and Bilge Qaghan (735) in the Orkhon valley carry the oldest long texts in the Old Turkic script, the first Turkic writing.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Tengri, the sky, gave the khagan his mandate; shamans and the sacred Ötüken forest stood at the center of belief.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Taspar Qaghan patronized Buddhism and had sutras translated into Turkic, though Tengri worship remained the rule.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The khaganate held the Silk Road from China to Persia, with Sogdian merchants as its traders and scribes.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Sogdian Maniakh, an envoy of the khagan, reached Constantinople to open a silk route around Sasanian Persia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Türk first appears in history with this empire.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Orkhon inscriptions remain the chief source for early Turkic language and history.
An alliance of Uyghur, Basmyl and Karluk tribes overthrew the khaganate; the Uyghur Khaganate rose in its place in 744.

passages.text: Goryeo, founded by Wang Geon in 918, ruled a united Korea from 936 and gave the country its name. Its Buddhist court produced jade-green celadon, the Tripitaka Koreana and the first books printed from metal type.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: A ritual text, the Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun, was printed from metal movable type by the record of the time, more than two centuries before Gutenberg; the Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed that way.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Tripitaka Koreana, the Buddhist canon in Chinese script, was carved on more than 81,000 wooden blocks between 1236 and 1251 as a prayer for deliverance from the Mongols.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Celadon with a jade-green glaze and inlaid black and white designs reached its height in the twelfth century.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist paintings on silk, gilt-bronze sculpture and sutras written in gold and silver on indigo paper.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Tripitaka blocks have been kept at Haeinsa temple since 1398 and can still be printed from after nearly 800 years.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism was the state faith, with temples, festivals and monks who held rank at court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations on the Chinese classics and composition began under King Gwangjong, with separate examinations for monks.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Korea comes from Goryeo, carried west by merchants and travelers.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Haeinsa's depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana were listed by UNESCO; the celadons are national treasures.
General Yi Seong-gye, who had turned his army back from a campaign against Ming in 1388, deposed the last Goryeo king and took the throne in 1392 as the founder of Joseon.

passages.text: Great Zimbabwe was a stone-built center created by ancestors of the Shona. Its surviving walls preserve part of a larger settlement of homes, courtyards and monumental enclosures.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders fitted local granite slabs together without mortar. Successive courses stepped inward, giving the curving walls a stabilizing inward slope.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Eight surviving soapstone bird sculptures combine human and bird features. Their precise meaning remains uncertain; an association with royal authority is one interpretation.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Stone walls stood beside homes made from daga, a building material of earth, with thatched roofs. Painted surfaces and enclosed courtyards formed parts of the lived settlement.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavations recovered imported glass beads, ceramics from China and Persia, and coins from Kilwa. These objects place the inland settlement within long-distance exchange networks; they do not, by themselves, identify every trader or route.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Six soapstone birds came from the Hill Complex's Eastern Enclosure. Their setting supports interpretations involving ritual or royal authority, but their original arrangement and precise meaning remain uncertain.

Great Zimbabwe did not simply empty in 1450. A study combining radiocarbon dates, stratigraphy and imported objects places occupation at least into the sixteenth century and probably the seventeenth, after its main building peak in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The chronology does not identify a single conquest or establish one cause for the loss of political prominence. The site remains a place of spiritual practice for contemporary communities; the decline of a capital did not mean the disappearance of its people.

passages.text: The Greek city-states formed a varied political and cultural world. These examples focus on Athens and Classical sculpture; Athenian institutions should not be assumed to describe every Greek community.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Athenian potters controlled the air admitted to a kiln in successive firing stages to produce contrasting black and red surfaces.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red-figure vase painting developed around 530 BCE. Brush-drawn details gave painters greater freedom to show anatomy, fabric and movement.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Polykleitos developed a system of bodily proportions. Many renowned Greek bronze compositions are known through later marble copies and written descriptions.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The marble Parthenon belonged to the building program associated with Perikles and the worship of Athena on the Athenian Acropolis.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: In Classical Athens, adult male citizens participated in the assembly. This was a particular civic institution, not political participation for every resident.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Different vessel shapes served storage, water carrying, drinking and ritual. Pottery images complement written evidence about Athenian life.

passages.text: Gunditjmara people maintain a living relationship with Country in south-western Victoria. At Budj Bim, generations shaped waterways into an aquaculture landscape. The map's imported date range describes its snapshots, not the beginning or end of Gunditjmara society.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, weirs and dams. These connected structures trapped, held and harvested kooyang, the short-finned eel.

passages.title: Science and environment
passages.text: Aquaculture depended on knowledge of seasonal eel movement, water flow and wetland ecology. Water management and food production were linked practices.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites alongside eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. Settlement and food processing belong in the same landscape.

passages.title: Arts and knowledge
passages.text: Storytelling, dance and basket weaving transmit knowledge across generations. Fibre baskets also belong to the practical technology of eel harvesting.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A cultural weir restored traditional flows into Tae Rak after earlier drainage. Gunditjmara customary responsibilities and cultural connections continue today.

passages.text: The Guptas ruled a large part of northern India during a period of influential mathematics, Sanskrit learning and religious art. Surviving temples, inscriptions and metalwork reveal the skills of craftspeople and the ambitions of patrons. These achievements belonged to a wider South Asian world: a work described as Gupta-period was not necessarily commissioned by a Gupta emperor.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: Aryabhata completed the Aryabhatiya at Kusumapura, usually associated with Pataliputra. It brings together mathematical rules and astronomical calculation, including a sine table and an approximation of pi equal to 3.1416.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: His method called kuttaka reduces problems about whole-number solutions to smaller steps. Such mathematics helped address astronomical questions about recurring planetary periods.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: Aryabhata used an alphabetic system to express numbers. Historians infer familiarity with place value, but that is different from a securely dated claim that he or the Gupta court invented the written zero.

passages.title: Metalworking and its surviving evidence
passages.text: The iron pillar now at Delhi's Qutb complex is associated with Chandragupta II. Its survival offers material evidence of skilled ironworking; its present location alone does not identify its original setting.

passages.title: Metalworking and its surviving evidence
passages.text: Analysis of the pillar's rust identified a protective layer containing iron phosphate. The study connects its unusual corrosion resistance to phosphorus in the iron and repeated wetting and drying, rather than to iron that never rusts.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: A sandstone seated Buddha from Uttar Pradesh, now at the Metropolitan Museum, is dated to the first quarter of the fifth century. It is a specific surviving example of Gupta-period sculpture; the collection record does not establish an excavated findspot.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: At Bhitargaon, builders used brick for a temple with a tall spire and terracotta panels of deities. India's heritage nomination dates it to the middle of the fifth century on stylistic grounds and leaves its dedication to Vishnu or Shiva unresolved.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: The early sixth-century temple at Deogarh preserves elaborate stone carving and part of its tower. Alongside Bhitargaon, it shows that builders developed temple forms in different materials, rather than following a single construction technique.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: Ajanta's later Buddhist caves belong to the same broad cultural period, but their patrons were Vakataka rulers and their feudatories. Their paintings should not be presented as a commission of the Gupta imperial court.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: The Mandsaur silk-weavers' inscription describes craftspeople moving from Lata to Dashapura with children and relatives. It preserves a community's account of migration and skilled work, although its praise of the city is commemorative poetry, not a household survey.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: The guild commemorated repairs to a Sun temple it had financed from its craft earnings. The inscription recalls the original foundation in 437 to 438 CE, showing artisans pooling resources for worship and maintenance across generations.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: Provincial and district officials governed alongside village institutions. Inscriptions also record trade guilds, while control of western ports connected the empire with overseas commerce. These institutions help explain the world beyond the royal court.

passages.title: Traditions beyond the dynasty
passages.text: Gupta-period sculptors developed Buddha images that influenced later Buddhist art across Asia. An artistic tradition could travel beyond the empire and outlast its rulers; the political endpoint of a dynasty is not the end of its cultural influence.

Gupta imperial rule broke apart through regional independence and repeated invasions, rather than one conquest by a single successor. Maitraka and Maukhari rulers were among the powers that emerged. Around 550 marks the conventional end of the imperial dynasty; communities and artistic traditions continued under changing governments.

passages.text: Under Hafsid rule, Tunis was a wealthy center of the western Islamic world. Its urban history joins markets, religious institutions and residential neighborhoods. The surviving medina contains work from several dynasties, so individual buildings require their own dates and patronage histories.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Northern and southern suburbs developed in the thirteenth century around the older central medina. Tunis was an expanding urban settlement, not only a palace city.

passages.title: Arts and exchange
passages.text: Tunis connected the Maghreb, southern Europe and lands to the east. These links encouraged exchanges in architecture and the arts.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Souqs, residential quarters and gates formed an interconnected townscape. Their survival helps historians study urban organization alongside individual monuments.

passages.title: Learning and beliefs
passages.text: Mosques and madrasas belonged to the city's institutional landscape. Surviving examples span both the Hafsid era and later periods.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Subsequent rulers added new palaces, residences and religious buildings. The medina records continuity and change across political transitions.

passages.text: The Han ruled China for four centuries, with a brief interruption, and set the pattern that later dynasties followed: an emperor advised by scholar-officials trained in the Confucian classics, a census-taking bureaucracy, and a capital laid out on a grid. Paper, the seismoscope and the first great history of China were made under the Han, and the Silk Road opened during their reign. The Chinese still call their majority people the Han.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Cai Lun presents the court with paper made from bark, hemp and rags. Paper travels west along the Silk Road and reaches Europe a thousand years later.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Zhang Heng builds a seismoscope: a bronze vessel that dropped a ball into one of eight dragon mouths to show the direction of a distant earthquake.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The wheelbarrow, the crank handle and the stern-mounted rudder are all first attested in Han China.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Taichu calendar reform sets the civil year, with its intercalary months, on the footing that Chinese calendars follow in principle to this day.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: systems of linear equations solved by a method equivalent to Gaussian elimination, rules for negative numbers, and an approximation of pi.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zhang Heng's water-driven armillary sphere turns with the heavens, and he catalogues about 2,500 stars.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Xu Shen's Shuowen Jiezi, the first dictionary to analyse Chinese characters by their components, is presented to the throne.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Du Shi harnesses a water wheel to the bellows of a blast furnace. Cast iron becomes cheap enough for ploughshares and hoes.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Brine wells drilled hundreds of meters deep with bamboo derricks in Sichuan, and natural gas piped through bamboo to boil the brine for salt.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Silk woven on multi-shaft treadle looms. Han silks have been found in Roman-era graves at Palmyra in Syria.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: The tombs at Mawangdui are sealed, preserving silk paintings, a silk map, and the earliest complete copies of the Daodejing.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: Sima Qian completes the Records of the Grand Historian, 130 chapters covering two thousand years and the model for every later Chinese dynastic history.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: The fu rhapsodies of Sima Xiangru, the folk songs collected by the Music Bureau, and lacquerware from Sichuan workshops exported across Asia.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Wu makes the Confucian classics the basis of official learning; the Imperial Academy follows in 124 BCE.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The White Horse Temple at Luoyang, by tradition China's first Buddhist temple, marks the arrival of Buddhism along the Silk Road.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Wang Chong's Lunheng argues that thunder is not the anger of heaven and that the dead have no consciousness.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zhang Daoling founds the Way of the Celestial Masters in Sichuan, the first organized Daoist religion.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zhang Qian sets out for the west. His reports of Ferghana horses, Parthia and India open what is now called the Silk Road.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Protectorate of the Western Regions is set up in the Tarim Basin, securing the route to Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: An embassy claiming to come from the Roman emperor Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) reaches the Han court by sea, according to the Book of Later Han.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The census counts 57,671,400 people, most of them farming households of about five on small plots of millet, wheat and rice, taxed in grain, cloth and labour.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Chang'an, the Western Han capital, sits inside about 25 km of walls with nine markets, and is one of the two largest cities in the world alongside Rome.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Games of liubo and cuju kickball, and the clay tomb figures of dancers, farmyards and watchtowers that show the Han world in miniature.

Weakened by court factions and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184, the dynasty ended when Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian in 220. China split into the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu.

passages.text: The Heian period was the high age of the Japanese court. With the Fujiwara regents running politics from Heian-kyo, the aristocracy turned to poetry, calligraphy and romance, and its women wrote the first great works of Japanese prose.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sei Shonagon finished The Pillow Book, her lists and observations of court life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The kana syllabaries took shape, so that Japanese could be written without Chinese.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Phoenix Hall of Byodoin at Uji was built for the Fujiwara, with its Amida by the sculptor Jocho.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Saicho founded Tendai on Mount Hiei and Kukai brought Shingon from China, the esoteric schools of the court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Genshin's Essentials of Rebirth spread devotion to Amida Buddha and the Pure Land.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The sensibility of mono no aware, the pathos of passing things, ran through court writing.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Aristocratic life turned on poetry contests, music, calligraphy, incense and love affairs conducted by letter.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Court women, writing in kana, produced the diaries and tales that define the age.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Tale of Genji remains at the center of Japanese literature.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The kana syllabaries are still the core of Japanese writing.
The Minamoto destroyed the Taira in the Genpei War, ending at Dan-no-ura in 1185; Minamoto no Yoritomo ruled from Kamakura and was named shogun in 1192.

passages.title: Diplomacy

passages.title: Food and daily life

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Clan Mothers help sustain ceremonies and teach younger generations. These are present-day responsibilities, not customs of a vanished society.

passages.text: Tawantinsuyu joined diverse Andean regions through roads, administration and local labor. Its infrastructure drew on earlier Andean traditions and adapted construction to mountains, valleys and coastal environments.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Road builders used bridges, stairs, paving and drainage suited to different terrain. The network linked centers of production, government and worship.

passages.title: Food and farming
passages.text: Communities built and maintained terraces that created level planting areas while resisting erosion. Water conduits also protected roads from damaging runoff.

passages.title: Water engineering
passages.text: Stone channels and storage facilities managed rainfall and snowmelt for resources shared among families.

passages.title: Storage
passages.text: Colcas were storehouses whose siting and construction kept supplies cool and dry. Their contents included potatoes, maize, quinoa, clothing and tools.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The road system moved goods including textiles, feathers, food and shell. It incorporated earlier routes and knowledge from Andean communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Andean languages and traditions continued under Spanish rule. Weavers combined established textile techniques and designs with new imagery.
Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532 and had him killed in 1533. Spanish conquest dismantled imperial government, while Andean peoples continued and adapted their traditions.

passages.text: The Jin dynasty briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, but internal weakness and uprisings by the peoples of the north led to the loss of the north in 316. The Eastern Jin survived in the south as a center of Chinese culture.

passages.text: Wang Xizhi writes the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion, the most admired piece of Chinese calligraphy, at a spring gathering of poets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Landscape painting begins to emerge as an independent art form; Gu Kaizhi paints the Admonitions scroll.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Huiyuan founds a Buddhist community on Mount Lu; translation projects and monasteries multiply.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Faxian sets out for India to collect Buddhist texts, and returns by sea fifteen years later.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, of the Wei to Jin transition, exemplify literati withdrawal and philosophical debate.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Eastern Jin preserved Chinese high culture in the south while the north underwent ethnic mixing.
The last Eastern Jin emperor abdicated to Liu Yu, a powerful general who founded the Liu Song dynasty.

passages.text: Joseon ruled Korea for more than five centuries under a Neo-Confucian order. King Sejong's court gave the country its alphabet, Hangul, and a run of scientific instruments; the dynasty survived Japanese and Manchu invasions and lasted, as the Korean Empire after 1897, until Japan annexed it in 1910.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: King Sejong created Hangul, published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, so that ordinary people could read and write.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The cheugugi rain gauge, a standard cylinder read against a ruler, was set up across the provinces, nearly two centuries before the first European rain gauge of 1639.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Jang Yeong-sil's self-striking water clock, the Jagyeongnu, and armillary spheres and sundials for the royal observatory.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Chiljeongsan calendar reform computed the motions of the sun, moon and planets for Seoul's own meridian.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Heo Jun's Donguibogam, a medical encyclopedia, was published.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: White porcelain, plain or painted in cobalt blue, became the ware of the scholar's table.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, a daily record of every reign from 1392 to 1863, among the longest continuous histories in the world.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Neo-Confucianism became state orthodoxy; Buddhism lost its land and court standing.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations on the Confucian classics selected officials, and the yangban scholar class ran the state.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships and cannon fleets cut the Japanese supply lines during the invasions of 1592 to 1598.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Gunpowder weapons, from hwacha rocket carts to ship-borne cannon, were made at state arsenals.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Hangul is the writing system of both Koreas today.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Neo-Confucian family and social values shaped Korean life for centuries.
Joseon was proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897 under the same royal house. Japan made it a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910.

passages.text: The Kamakura period brought Japan's first warrior government. The shogunate at Kamakura ruled beside the old court in Kyoto, the samurai became the ruling class, and new Buddhist schools, Zen among them, reached both warriors and common people.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Eisai brought Rinzai Zen from Song China, and Dogen founded Soto Zen in 1227; meditation and discipline appealed to the warriors.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Honen's Pure Land school, then Shinran's True Pure Land and Nichiren's Lotus school of 1253, offered salvation to ordinary people.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Warrior ideals of loyalty and service took shape, later codified as bushido.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Unkei and the Kei school carved lifelike portraits of monks and guardian figures with inlaid crystal eyes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Great Buddha of Kamakura, a bronze Amida more than 11 meters high, was cast.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Emaki handscrolls told war tales and temple legends; ink painting arrived with the Zen monks.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Samurai held land as vassals of the shogun and lived by the sword and the bow.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The court in Kyoto kept its ceremonies and titles while Kamakura held the armies and the law.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Mongol invasion fleets were repelled in 1274 and 1281, the second wrecked by a typhoon later called the kamikaze.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Shoguns governed Japan for nearly 700 years, until 1868.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zen shaped Japanese gardens, tea, ink painting and the martial arts.
Forces loyal to Emperor Go-Daigo took Kamakura in 1333. Ashikaga Takauji turned on the emperor and set up a new shogunate in Kyoto in 1336, the start of the Muromachi period.

passages.text: Kerma was the capital of a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its prosperity rested on herding, cultivation and exchange between African interiors and Egypt. This page follows the kingdom, its earlier background and what archaeology reveals about its people.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavators mapped houses with courtyards containing kitchens and grain silos. These remains show how households organized cooking and storage around shared outdoor space.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Temple workshops and storerooms clustered around the Western Deffufa. A palace contained a large circular building interpreted as a royal audience hall, revealing distinct religious and political spaces.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Middle Kerma grave 253, researchers recorded 4,899 cattle skulls. They interpret the association between large tombs and numerous skulls as a display of the deceased person's wealth and power.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Some cattle horns had been deliberately reshaped; cut marks and altered growth preserve evidence of the practice. Researchers suggest specially valued animals were distinguished this way, while warning against copying modern herders' beliefs directly onto ancient Kerma.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Kerma potters shaped exceptionally thin cups by hand, then polished their red surfaces. Controlled firing produced black rims and interiors, evidence of skilled handling of both clay and the firing atmosphere.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: A tulip-shaped beaker in Manchester Museum was excavated at Kerma in 1913. Its smooth, shining finish was made by burnishing the clay before firing; the form was achieved without a potter's wheel.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Cattle also appeared in small figurines found in the city and in paintings in a funerary chapel. Their presence in art as well as graves suggests a significance extending beyond food and exchange.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Animal bones from the capital show that domestic livestock supplied most of the meat evidence. Cattle, sheep and goats dominated; the researchers observed a later increase in sheep and goats relative to cattle.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Fine beakers existed alongside heavier storage jars, sometimes stamped around the rim. Stone implements remained in use beside metal technology, preserving evidence of practical choices in everyday tools.

passages.title: Burial, belief and social rank
passages.text: Graves preserve wooden beds, personal ornaments, sandals and containers for oils or ointments. Larger, richer tombs show growing inequality; some also contained accompanying people interpreted as victims of funerary killing.

passages.title: Trade and cultural connections
passages.text: A Kerma-style beaker now at the Metropolitan Museum was excavated at Abydos in Egypt. Such finds demonstrate connections across the Nile Valley, but the museum cautions that pottery alone cannot establish whether the people buried with it were Nubian traders.

passages.title: What continued after conquest
passages.text: Survey finds include Egyptian pottery together with Nubian pottery. Stuart Tyson Smith interprets the settlement pattern as evidence that some local elites retained cultural and political latitude under Egyptian rule; conquest did not erase Nubian society.

passages.title: What remains uncertain
passages.text: The relationship between the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement and the royal city is not fully demonstrated. Excavated buildings and objects reveal much, but their locations do not establish precise kingdom borders.

Egyptian New Kingdom campaigns ended Kerma's independence. The excavation mission places the capital's destruction around 1450 BCE, after a longer conquest associated with Thutmose I and Thutmose III; this is an approximate endpoint, not a known single day of collapse.
