passages.text: The Hawaiian Kingdom joined islands with much older political and cultural traditions. Its people developed newspapers, constitutional institutions and international connections while maintaining knowledge of land, water and the arts. This card follows the monarchy from Kamehameha I's consolidation in 1795 to its overthrow in 1893; unification of the principal islands was completed in 1810.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: At Heeia, parallel basalt walls packed mainly with coral slowed the movement of water. Sluice gates controlled freshwater and seawater flows, maintaining brackish conditions in which algae could feed herbivorous fish. This engineering tradition long predates the unified kingdom.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: Fishponds helped maintain a food supply when rough seas interrupted ocean fishing. Heeia remained part of the kingdom's lived landscape: Abner Paki received much of the surrounding land during the Mahele of 1848.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: Ka Lama Hawaii began publication at Lahainaluna Seminary on Maui in 1834. Surviving issues preserve Hawaiian-language writing from the kingdom itself, giving readers access to contemporary voices alongside later histories.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A letter from Hanalei printed in Ka Hae Hawaii on 14 January 1857 set out Hawaiian month names and day counts. Its author, J. W. Q. Kaia, worried that younger readers no longer knew them. The museum cautions that month names varied between islands.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A surviving Ka Nupepa Kuokoa issue displays the Hawaiian flag in color on 1 January 1862. The original held at Hamilton Library is evidence of printing and national expression that can be lost in poor reproductions; conservation and digitization make such details easier to study.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The Kuhina Nui shared governing authority with the monarch, including land distribution, treaties and justice. Women of high chiefly rank held the office first. Calling it simply a prime ministership understates the authority of these early co-regents.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The constitution of 1840 provided for a council of nobles and a representative body chosen by the people. Early legislative rules developed over time; a written constitution did not immediately create equal political power for everyone.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: Lahaina linked local households with visiting whaling ships, trade and, later, sugar plantations. From the 1850s Chinese immigrants worked under plantation contracts, and some settled on Maui after those contracts ended. The kingdom's economic history includes these workers as well as its rulers.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Completed in 1882, Iolani Palace combined a royal home with rooms for official receptions and visiting dignitaries. Hula performances and grand balls formed part of its public and ceremonial life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Liliuokalani composed Aloha Oe in 1878, before becoming queen. Her work as a composer forms part of a larger musical legacy remembered alongside her political life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: In 1886 Liliuokalani founded an educational society to support schooling for Hawaiian girls with limited means. Her public work connected royal patronage with access to education beyond the court.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: The Highways Act of 1892 protected public trails and rights of access. Its continuing importance to Hawaiian trail preservation shows how a kingdom-era law can shape the landscape after a change of government.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: A royalist attempt to restore Liliuokalani in 1895 failed. She was tried in the palace throne room and confined in an upstairs room, turning the royal residence into a place of imprisonment.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Hawaiians organized petitions against annexation in 1897, and Liliuokalani continued to protest. These records preserve organized political opposition after the monarchy had been overthrown.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Congress passed its annexation resolution on 7 July 1898. This later US action must be distinguished from the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893.

On 17 January 1893, the Committee of Safety overthrew Liliuokalani with support from the US minister and US Marines, establishing a Provisional Government. A republic followed in 1894. The removal of the monarchy did not end Hawaiian people, culture or opposition to annexation.

passages.text: The Kuba kingdom brought together several principalities in Central Africa. Royal and aristocratic patronage encouraged inventive textiles, carved vessels and images through which rank and historical memory became visible.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Kuba makers wove raffia palm fibers into cloth. Women joined, dyed and embellished panels with embroidery and applique.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cutting embroidered raffia threads created a dense pile surface. Some panels were displayed as prestige objects and used as currency rather than worn.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Multiple cloth panels formed wrappers whose gathered edges moved with the wearer. Dress combined bodily movement with elaborate surface design.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Ndop sculptures memorialized rulers through idealized seated figures and identifying symbols. A strategy board identifies Shyaam aMbul aNgoong.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Kuba chronologies preserve references to a solar eclipse and Halley's comet, giving historians points for comparison with independently dated celestial events.

passages.text: Kush was an African kingdom of the Middle Nile whose centers included Napata and Meroe. Its rulers and craftspeople developed distinctive monuments while exchanging ideas with neighboring societies. The royal city, religious settlements and industrial remains show a civilization extending well beyond its famous pyramids.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron-working remains and ceramic production areas at Meroe document skilled manufacture. They establish local production, not a claim that Kush invented iron smelting.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Reservoirs helped support settlements away from the Nile. Their remains are evidence for both engineering and the environmental conditions in which people lived.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Steep-sided pyramids, decorated funerary chapels and painted burial chambers gave Kushite royal commemoration a distinctive appearance.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Architecture at Meroe, Naqa and Musawwarat combined Kushite forms with elements associated with Egypt, Greece and Rome.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Gebel Barkal was a sacred landscape. Temples at its foot connected royal authority with the worship of Amun.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Meroitic political order ended in late antiquity, but burial traditions continued afterward. A kingdom's disappearance should not be read as the disappearance of its people.

passages.text: The Kushans, a Yuezhi clan from Bactria, built an empire from the Oxus to the Ganges in the first three centuries CE. They struck gold coins, stood at the crossing of the Silk Road, and under Kanishka became the great patrons of Buddhism and the art of Gandhara.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gandharan sculptors, drawing on Greek and Roman models, made some of the first images of the Buddha in human form, at the same time as the workshops of Mathura.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stupas and monasteries rose at Taxila, Peshawar and Hadda; Chinese pilgrims reported Kanishka's stupa at Peshawar as the tallest building they had seen.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The empire held the passes between the Silk Road, the Indus ports and the Ganges plain, and traded with Rome by sea and with Han China by land.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold coins on the Roman weight standard, showing Greek, Iranian, Indian and Buddhist gods, circulated from Central Asia to the Ganges.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Kanishka's reign, beginning about 127 CE, is remembered in Buddhist tradition for a council in Kashmir that fixed the canon of the Sarvastivada school.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zoroastrian, Greek, Hindu and Buddhist deities all appear on Kushan coins, and Bactrian, written in Greek letters, was the language of the state.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Gandharan Buddhist art traveled along the Silk Road to Central Asia and China.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Kushan patronage helped carry Buddhism to Central Asia and on to China.
The Sasanians took Bactria and the west in the third century and set up Kushano-Sasanian governors; the last Kushan kings ruled in the Punjab in the shadow of the Guptas until about 375.

passages.text: Later Liang was the first of the Five Dynasties that ruled northern China between the Tang and Song. Founded by Zhu Wen, a former rebel who deposed the last Tang emperor, it controlled only part of northern China and faced constant military threats.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kaifeng developed as the capital, though smaller and less cosmopolitan than Tang Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Five Dynasties period saw the rise of military strongmen who dominated politics.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Printing technology continued to develop during this unstable period.
Li Cunxu of Later Tang conquered Later Liang and captured its capital Kaifeng in 923.

passages.text: The Liu Song was the first of the Southern Dynasties, ruling from Jiankang. Despite political instability, this period saw significant cultural and intellectual achievements in the south.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi proposes the Daming calendar, the first in China to allow for the precession of the equinoxes.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi (429 to 500) bounds pi between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, a precision not bettered anywhere for about nine centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The poet Xie Lingyun (385 to 433) develops landscape poetry as a major genre.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Southern culture developed distinctive characteristics that influenced later periods.
The last Liu Song emperor was deposed by Xiao Daocheng, who founded the Southern Qi dynasty.

passages.title: Knowledge and memory
passages.text: Lukasa boards use carved forms or attached beads and shells to organize histories, genealogies and significant places. Their interpretation depends on trained specialists.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The mbudye association includes women and men who interpret political principles and can restrain or reinforce chiefly authority.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Female figures on royal seats, staffs and other court objects relate to ancestral kings and the sacred character of rule.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Carved headrests protected elaborate hairstyles while their owners slept. A nineteenth-century example repeats the hairstyle in the sculpture itself.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A headrest can create a strong sculptural composition with slender limbs and open spaces while still supporting the sleeper's head.

passages.text: Lunda rulers adapted aspects of Luba kingship while maintaining their own political independence. Trade routes and relationships with neighboring courts supported the movement of materials, artistic forms and political ideas.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: By 1650, Mwaant Yaav Naweej had connected his capital with Atlantic trade. This commerce included enslaved people as well as forest products.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Lunda outposts participated in copper exchange, while settlements near Lake Mweru linked the interior with eastern commercial routes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rulers commissioned artists from client peoples, including Chokwe carvers, to make prestigious court objects.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Accounts of Chibinda Ilunga describe a founding culture hero. They are traditions of legitimacy, not a dated eyewitness biography.

passages.title: Music and memory
passages.text: In related Chokwe court art, a chief holds a lamellophone associated with historical recitation and praise. The object shows how music and political knowledge could meet.

passages.text: Majapahit, founded in eastern Java in 1293, was the last great Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of the archipelago. Under Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada it claimed overlordship from Sumatra to the Moluccas and set the pattern that Indonesia's founders looked back to.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Nagarakretagama, a poem by Mpu Prapanca finished in 1365, describes the court, the royal progress and the lands that sent tribute.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red brick temples and gateways at Trowulan, and terracotta figures and piggy banks from the capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wayang shadow plays and gamelan are named in Majapahit texts and carved on its reliefs.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Javanese rice bought the cloves, nutmeg and mace of the Moluccas, which Majapahit ships carried west.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Chinese cash coins were the currency; missions went to the Ming court, and Chinese and Muslim traders lived in the ports.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shiva and the Buddha were worshipped together; the court poem Sutasoma's line Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, unity in diversity, is Indonesia's motto.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The realm was a mandala of vassals around a divine king, held by ritual and tribute more than by garrisons.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Indonesia's founders invoked Majapahit's reach when they drew the nation's borders.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Its Hindu-Javanese culture lives on in Bali, where nobles and priests moved as Islam spread in Java.
The kingdom shrank after Hayam Wuruk's death in 1389 and a civil war; the Muslim sultanate of Demak took the last Majapahit capital around 1527.

passages.text: Malacca, founded about 1400 by Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, became within a century the greatest port of Asia, where the monsoons met. Its sultans made Islam and Malay the faith and language of the archipelago's trade.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Ships from China, Gujarat, Bengal, Arabia, Java and the Spice Islands met at Malacca to exchange cloth, spices, tin, gold and porcelain.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tomé Pires, writing just after the conquest, counted 84 languages spoken in the city and wrote that whoever was lord of Malacca had his hand on the throat of Venice.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zheng He's fleets called at Malacca from 1405, and the sultanate sent missions to the Ming court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ruler adopted Islam around 1414, taking the name Iskandar Shah; Malacca became a center from which Islam spread to Java and the islands.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Undang-Undang Melaka, the laws of Malacca, and the Malay Annals were written in Malay in the Arabic script.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malay spread as the lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia and became Malaysian and Indonesian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malacca's laws and court customs set the model for the Malay sultanates.
Afonso de Albuquerque took the city in August 1511 after a month's fighting; the sultan fled and his heirs founded Johor.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold and salt served long-distance commerce; cowrie shells also entered local exchange during the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Mansa Musa passed through Cairo during his pilgrimage in 1324 to 1325. His distribution of gold made a strong impression on contemporaries.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Timbuktu's Djingareyber Mosque traces its initial construction to Musa's return from pilgrimage. Later rebuilding means the surviving fabric represents multiple periods.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Mande jeliw transmit historical epics through skilled performance. Musical accompaniment helps structure and pace narratives.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mosque architecture and scholarship connected Timbuktu to Islamic networks while local building practices remained central.

passages.text: Maori society comprises distinct iwi and hapu with their own histories and authority. This card introduces shared themes while preserving those differences. The imported map interval is not an extinction date: Maori communities, language and cultural institutions continue.

passages.title: Agriculture
passages.text: Growers adapted horticulture to a cooler climate, using techniques including stone walls and warmed soils to cultivate kumara. Practices varied with local environments.

passages.title: Technology and exchange
passages.text: Pounamu and obsidian supplied tool materials; harakeke supplied fibre. Gift exchange helped move valued materials among communities.

passages.title: Ideas and governance
passages.text: Local groups exercised their own authority. Genealogy connected individuals to wider communities, while tapu and mana shaped relationships with people and natural resources.

passages.title: Science and seasons
passages.text: For many iwi, the midwinter appearance of Matariki marked the new year. Observances differ among iwi and include remembering the dead and sharing the harvest.

passages.text: The Maratha state founded by Shivaji in the Western Ghats broke Mughal power in the eighteenth century and, as a confederacy of chiefs under the Peshwa at Pune, ruled or taxed most of India by the 1750s. Its horsemen, hill forts and revenue administration made it the last great Indian power before the British.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Light cavalry that lived off the country and struck and withdrew defeated slower Mughal armies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Shivaji's chain of hill forts, Raigad, Pratapgad and Sinhagad among them, controlled the passes of the Western Ghats.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A navy under Kanhoji Angre held the Konkan coast against the Portuguese, the Siddis and the East India Company.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in a Vedic ceremony asserting independent Hindu kingship.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Ashtapradhan, a council of eight ministers, ran war, revenue, foreign affairs and religion.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Marathi, with Sanskrit terms replacing Persian ones in Shivaji's chancery, became the language of state.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Revenue came as chauth and sardeshmukhi, a quarter and a tenth of the yield, collected directly from the land.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Maratha wars drained the Mughals; after the defeat at Panipat in 1761 the confederacy recovered and held Delhi's emperor as a client.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Marathi identity and the memory of Shivaji remain central in Maharashtra.
The East India Company beat the confederacy in three wars; the Peshwa surrendered in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War and his lands were annexed.

passages.text: Maya history encompasses distinct societies and city-states. Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copan supported royal courts with specialized artists; their political histories should be explored individually rather than compressed into one Maya empire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Some court artists signed their work. The sculptor Chakalte' left his name on a relief showing Shield Jaguar IV receiving tribute.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Stoneworkers carved and polished limestone vessels with tools and abrasives. Shell, bone, jade and fired clay offered other media for intricate objects.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Blue-green jade evoked water, new growth and primordial beings. It became material for offerings, ornaments and royal regalia.

passages.title: Writing and history
passages.text: Tikal's carved and painted inscriptions preserve dynastic history and relationships with other cities. They document particular courts, not a single pan-Maya government.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Tikal combined monumental precincts with residential districts and reservoirs known today as aguadas. Its surrounding settlements also supported agricultural production.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: After several Classic-period kingdoms declined, northern centers such as Chichen Itza continued commissioning major artworks. Political collapse in one region did not end Maya history everywhere.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Tikal's Corriental reservoir, researchers identified zeolite and coarse quartz in dated sediment layers. They interpret these minerals as evidence of a water filter; its proposed stone supports and woven matting are a reconstruction, not a surviving intact installation.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Water-jar fragments occur throughout Corriental's excavated sediment sequence, linking the reservoir to everyday water collection. The filter evidence comes from this particular reservoir, not from every Maya city.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Copan, exposed layers of the Acropolis preserve earlier plaza floors and covered water outlets beneath later construction. These buried surfaces reveal repeated rebuilding of the city rather than a monument created in a single episode.

Maya societies did not share one fall date or one conqueror. UNESCO places Copan's abandonment in the early tenth century, while northern centers continued major artistic production after many Classic courts declined; a local city's decline cannot stand for the end of all Maya societies. Maya communities continue today, with living languages and cultural traditions.

passages.text: Mercia was a kingdom in central England. Large earthworks and the Staffordshire Hoard offer different views of its region: organized construction and highly skilled early medieval metalwork.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Offa's Dyke used a bank and ditch to mark a frontier. English Heritage dates its construction probably to the 780s.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Staffordshire Hoard fragments include intricate gold and garnet decoration. Their designs have connections across several European regions.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Many hoard fragments belonged to an elaborate helmet. Modern reconstruction relies on study of the surviving pieces rather than discovery of an intact helmet.

passages.title: Evidence and daily life
passages.text: The hoard reveals elite craftsmanship and equipment. Its burial location alone cannot identify every maker or make it a representative sample of ordinary Mercian households.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Scholars from Mercia contributed to the translations supported by Alfred of Wessex. Learned activity crossed the boundaries between neighboring kingdoms.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Fez Jedid was founded in 1276 beside Fez el-Bali. It included the palace, fortifications, military headquarters and residential districts.

passages.title: Learning and beliefs
passages.text: Madrasas and mosques are among the principal monuments associated with the city's Marinid flourishing in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

passages.title: Daily life and trade
passages.text: Fondouks, houses and fountains belonged to the capital's urban fabric alongside royal and religious buildings.

passages.title: Arts and legacy
passages.text: Fez's architecture brought local skills into conversation with influences from Andalusia and other African and eastern centers. Its craft traditions continued beyond any one dynasty.

passages.text: Minoan is the modern name for Bronze Age Cretan culture, with several palatial centers rather than one securely documented island-wide kingdom. Its crafts, exchange networks and administrative writing linked Crete to the wider Mediterranean.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Mallia and Zakros grouped rooms around central courts. Lighting, ventilation and sanitary facilities formed part of their design.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Cretan hieroglyphic writing and Linear A appear on administrative tablets and ritual objects. Palace record keeping helped organize economic activity.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall paintings show rituals and the natural world. Jewelers worked with filigree and granulation, while engravers carved seal stones.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: A small agate gem in the Met depicts a griffin and is dated approximately 1450 to 1400 BCE. Objects preserve artistic continuity beyond a single palace destruction.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Crete exported timber, textiles, food and luxury crafts, while importing metals and other raw materials.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Widespread destruction around 1450 BCE accompanied growing Mycenaean influence. Linear B administration and mixed pottery styles followed; neither the destruction nor cultural change has a securely identified single cause.

passages.text: Moche societies flourished along Peru's northern coastal valleys during the first through eighth centuries CE. Their ceramics preserve an unusually rich visual record of people, animals, plants and ritual activity.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Potters used molds to produce standardized vessel shapes while varying their painted and sculpted decoration.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Many vessels combine red and cream slip painting with modeled figures. Complex scenes could cover the surface of a stirrup-spout bottle.

passages.title: Portraiture
passages.text: Portrait bottles may depict recognizable individuals. Scholars debate how their social identities related to the vessels' eventual placement in burials.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Fine decorated pottery also occurs in residential compounds. Wear, repairs and excavated household contexts show that many vessels served the living before burial.

passages.title: Food and gatherings
passages.text: Decorated vessels participated in household rituals and feasts, including the sharing of food and corn beer.

passages.title: How we know
passages.text: Images include crops, animals, healers and supernatural beings. They are a visual source, but an image alone cannot tell us every detail of the activity it depicts.

passages.text: The Nara period gave Japan its first permanent capital, Heijo-kyo, laid out on the grid of the Tang capital Chang'an. The court ran the country under the ritsuryo codes, made Buddhism a state religion and compiled its first histories and poetry.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Manyoshu, an anthology of 4,516 poems by emperors, courtiers and frontier guards, was compiled; its latest dated poem is from 759.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Kojiki, and in 720 the Nihon Shoki, recorded the myths and early history of the imperial line.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Great Buddha of Todaiji, a bronze figure about 15 meters high, was dedicated in a ceremony attended by monks from India and China.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Shomu ordered a state temple and nunnery in every province.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ritsuryo codes, the Taiho of 701 and the Yoro of 718, organized government, taxes and land on Tang models.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning was taught at the state academy to train officials.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Chinese characters were used for all government records, and census and tax registers were kept on paper.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Trunk roads with post stations linked the capital to the provinces.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Manyoshu remains the foundation of Japanese poetry.
Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, in 794, the start of the Heian period.

passages.title: Technology

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Truus Schroder-Schrader commissioned the house designed by Gerrit Rietveld in Utrecht in 1924. Its design expressed ideas associated with De Stijl.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Schroder House used a flexible internal arrangement so rooms could change with their functions. Furniture and interior space were treated as parts of one design.

passages.text: The Yungang cave temples carved near Datong, with massive Buddha statues.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Xiaowen moves the capital to Luoyang and orders the Xianbei to adopt Chinese language, dress and surnames; work on the Longmen caves begins the year before.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The equal-field system implemented, distributing land to peasant households.

passages.title: Legacy

passages.title: Legacy

passages.text: King Oswald invited Aidan from Iona to establish a monastery at Lindisfarne in 635. Royal support placed the foundation near the kingdom's political center.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Lindisfarne Gospels were made approximately 710 to 725. They are evidence of the monastery's role as a center of Christian learning and book production.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Pilgrims came to Cuthbert's shrine, while patrons gave land, money and precious objects. Religious devotion helped support the monastery's economy.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Runic name stones commemorate Anglo-Saxon inhabitants of Lindisfarne, preserving writing outside the pages of books.

passages.title: Change and continuity

passages.text: Numidian society belongs to North Africa's indigenous history and its wider Mediterranean connections. Thugga, now Dougga, offers evidence for urban life under Numidian kings and for its transformation under Roman rule. The spectacular Roman monuments there are later additions to an older town.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: At Thugga, Roman construction was fitted into a largely Numidian street pattern. Urban continuity survived the change of political authority.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Libyan, Punic and bilingual inscriptions help reconstruct Numidian social and municipal life. Their study also contributed to deciphering Libyan writing.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Libyco-Punic mausoleum preserves an important pre-Roman monumental tradition, although its modern reconstruction complicates interpretation of the standing structure.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Under Rome, an indigenous community and a legally distinct group of Roman citizens coexisted at Thugga. Cultural change did not require the town's earlier inhabitants to vanish.

passages.text: Olmec names a group of early Mesoamerican societies, especially those of Mexico's Gulf Coast. Their monumental building projects and stoneworking joined local farming communities to far-reaching networks of materials and artistic ideas.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At San Lorenzo, communities cooperated to build large earthen platforms and mounds. These were shared construction projects beyond the needs of individual households.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Artists worked both enormous volcanic-stone sculptures and small, finely finished jade objects. Those materials could travel from distant sources.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maize farming helped sustain communities in Gulf Coast river valleys, although many details of San Lorenzo's households remain under investigation.

passages.title: Games
passages.text: Rubber balls recovered at El Manati provide early evidence for the place of ballgames in Olmec life.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: La Venta's carvings connect rulers with watery environments and agricultural fertility. Their imagery draws on the surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: La Venta flourished especially between 1000 and 500 BCE and was apparently abandoned by 400 BCE. That local sequence does not establish one universal fall for all Olmec societies.

passages.text: The Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy used Ravenna as a royal center. Its surviving buildings and personal ornaments show both distinctive traditions and close engagement with the Roman world.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Theodoric's mausoleum used large blocks of Istrian stone arranged around a central space.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sant'Apollinare Nuovo began as Theodoric's palace chapel. Its mosaics combined Roman traditions with eastern Mediterranean influence.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Arian Baptistery preserves imagery expressing the court's Christian faith. The Archbishop's Chapel represents a different Christian community in the same city.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: In wider Ostrogothic dress, pairs of shoulder brooches secured women's long garments. Decorated belts, necklaces and other jewelry completed the ensemble.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A surviving brooch attributed to wider Ostrogothic material culture was cast in silver, with silver covering its copper-alloy pin. It combined practical fastening and ornament; the record does not establish manufacture in Italy.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Ravenna passed from Ostrogothic to Byzantine rule. Buildings surviving together today belong to different patrons and periods; San Vitale's Justinianic decoration should not be credited to Theodoric.

passages.text: The kingdom of Pagan, on the Irrawaddy, united the Burmese lands under Anawrahta in the 1050s and made Theravada Buddhism the faith of the country. Its kings and people covered the plain of Bagan with thousands of temples in two hundred years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: More than 2,000 temples and stupas still stand at Bagan out of some 10,000 built between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Ananda temple, finished about 1105 under Kyansittha, with its four standing Buddhas and gilded spire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Burmese writing, adapted from the Mon script, appears on the Myazedi inscription of 1113 beside Pyu, Mon and Pali.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Anawrahta adopted Theravada Buddhism under the Mon monk Shin Arahan and in 1057 took Thaton, bringing its monks and scriptures to Pagan.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Contacts with Sri Lanka in the twelfth century renewed the monastic ordination and the Pali canon.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Weirs and canals in the Kyaukse district fed the rice that paid for the temples.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Bagan was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism remains the religion of most of Myanmar.

Mongol armies invaded in 1277 and 1287, and King Narathihapate fled and was murdered by his own son. His successors ruled as Mongol vassals until the three brothers of Myinsaing deposed the last of them in 1297.

passages.text: The Parthian Empire, ruled by the Arsacid dynasty from 247 BCE to 224 CE, held Iran and Mesopotamia between Rome and the steppe for nearly five centuries. Its armored lancers and horse archers, its great noble houses and its grip on the Silk Road made it Rome's only equal in the East.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Parthian shot: horse archers turned in the saddle to shoot behind them at full gallop.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Carrhae in 53 BCE, horse archers and cataphracts, riders and horses in scale armor, destroyed a Roman army under Crassus.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The empire sat astride the Silk Road; Chinese silk reached Rome through Parthian middlemen who kept the two ends apart.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Envoys from Han China reached the Parthian court in the 110s BCE, and in 97 CE the Han envoy Gan Ying got as far as the Persian Gulf.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zoroastrian, Greek, Babylonian and Jewish communities kept their own cults, and the kings styled themselves friends of the Greeks on their coins.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Arsacids claimed descent from the Achaemenid king Artaxerxes II.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Sasanians inherited Parthian cavalry, provinces and great noble houses.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Parthian, a Middle Iranian language written in its own script, was still used in the Sasanian royal inscriptions.
Ardashir I of Persis defeated and killed the last Arsacid king, Artabanus IV, at Hormozdgan in 224 and founded the Sasanian dynasty.

passages.text: This chapter follows Portuguese architecture and learning from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, through Lisbon's Belem complex and Coimbra's colleges, laboratories and printing facilities.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: In sixteenth-century Belem, the Hieronymites monastery combined richly carved Manueline decoration with spaces for worship, meals, study and communal life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Belem tower incorporated ribbed cupolas inspired by Islamic architecture. Its design records artistic exchange across cultural boundaries.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs

passages.title: Technology

passages.title: Arts

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs

passages.text: The Ptolemies governed Egypt from Alexandria as Macedonian monarchs and Egyptian pharaohs. Their kingdom brought Greek-speaking rulers into a society with enduring Egyptian languages, temples and crafts. Surviving decrees and estate papers reveal both royal institutions and everyday work.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: The Rosetta Stone preserves a priestly decree honoring Ptolemy V in 196 BCE. Soldiers found it reused in a fort at el-Rashid in 1799, so its discovery location is not the original setting of the decree.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: Hieroglyphic Egyptian, Demotic Egyptian and Greek versions address different readers of the same royal decree. This is evidence of multilingual administration and priestly authority, not three different spoken languages.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: Villagers digging for fertilizer uncovered the Zenon archive near ancient Philadelphia in 1914 to 1915. The documents illuminate a third-century BCE estate, but their exact original findspot was not recorded.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: A lease copied in a lawsuit prepared by Zenon required tenants to grow wheat and barley and deliver grain rent at Philadelphia. Clauses about seed advances and outstanding debts reveal how agricultural work depended on both produce and credit.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: The same document allowed recovery from debtors, their guarantors and their property. Read beside its crop instructions, it shows the unequal bargaining power behind estate production, rather than an idyllic picture of farming.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: A papyrus dated 7 May 254 BCE records a stolen donkey. This small dispute survives because estate papers were kept, giving a glimpse of transport animals and ordinary losses outside royal histories.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: Eratosthenes worked at the Alexandrian library in the third century BCE. He compared summer-solstice shadows at Syene and Alexandria with an estimated distance between them to calculate Earth's circumference.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: His original measurement treatise is lost; the method survives in later authors. Uncertainty about the length of the stadium makes a single modern claim for his percentage accuracy misleading.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: The sieve associated with Eratosthenes identifies prime numbers by removing multiples. It is a concrete example of mathematical reasoning connected with Alexandria's scholarly world.

passages.title: Arts and religious life
passages.text: Temple workshops made faience vessels and colorful glass inlays. Egyptian and Greek forms coexisted, and royal portraits could combine Greek hair with Egyptian poses.

passages.title: Arts and religious life
passages.text: Egyptian temples remained centers of scholarship and worship, supported by rulers who also promoted their own royal cults.

passages.title: Trade and correspondence
passages.text: Zenon's files include letters about shipments of wheat and wine as well as official and personal business. Their survival connects agricultural production with transport and administration, rather than treating trade as an abstract royal achievement.
Roman takeover in 30 BCE ended the dynasty after Cleopatra VII's defeat. Egyptian religious and artistic traditions continued beyond the change of rulers.

passages.text: Pueblo societies comprise distinct communities and histories. Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde preserve ancestral building and farming landscapes; Taos Pueblo is a living community with its own traditions and government.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: At Chaco, builders planned multistory Great Houses whose construction could span generations. Their masonry and shared layouts mark a regional architectural tradition.

passages.title: Science and landscape
passages.text: Many Chaco structures were oriented toward solar, lunar or cardinal directions. Their placement linked buildings to a meaningful surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mesa Verde preserves farming terraces, check dams, reservoirs and ditches as well as houses. These remains document the engineering of everyday subsistence.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Roads connected Chaco Great Houses across the region. Some major buildings may have hosted periodic ceremonies and exchange rather than dense permanent populations.

passages.title: Living architecture
passages.text: At Taos, families maintain adobe homes by renewing earthen plaster. Taos describes that work as an ongoing connection between ancestors and the present.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Changes in ancestral settlements did not end Pueblo life. Mesa Verde remains a living connection to present-day Pueblo peoples, and Taos continues as a sovereign community.

passages.text: Qin began as a frontier state of the Zhou in the Wei River valley in 770 BCE and grew, by reform and conquest, into the power that unified China in 221 BCE. The empire created a centralized bureaucratic state that replaced feudal fragmentation. Though the dynasty lasted only fifteen years, its institutional innovations became the foundation of all subsequent Chinese empires.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shang Yang's reforms in the state of Qin reward farming and soldiering, punish by fixed law and break the power of the old nobility, the Legalist programme the empire would follow.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Legalism becomes state orthodoxy, emphasizing strict laws, harsh punishments and absolute state power.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Books of rival philosophies are ordered burned, and by tradition scholars are executed the next year.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The First Emperor seeks immortality through alchemy and travels to sacred mountains.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Standardization of weights, measures, axle widths and written script across the empire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Construction of the Great Wall begins, connecting earlier defensive walls along the northern frontier.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Terracotta Army, some 8,000 life-size soldiers, is completed to guard the First Emperor's tomb; work had begun on his accession in 246 BCE.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze mirrors, crossbow mechanisms and standardized coinage show unified artistic standards.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The small seal script standardized for official use, later replaced by clerical script.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The empire divided into thirty-six commanderies governed by appointed officials rather than hereditary lords.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Corvée labor conscripted for massive public works: roads, the Lingqu canal linking the Yangzi and Pearl river systems, and the Epang palace.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Harsh legal code applied uniformly across the empire.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Standardized bronze coins in round shape with square hole become the empire's currency.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imperial highways facilitate military movement and commercial exchange.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name China probably derives from Qin, by way of Sanskrit and Persian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Centralized bureaucratic administration replaced feudalism in all subsequent dynasties.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Standardized writing enabled cultural unity across linguistic diversity.
After the First Emperor's death, popular rebellions and civil war led to the dynasty's collapse in 206 BCE; Liu Bang, the victor of the wars that followed, founded the Han.

passages.text: For four centuries one government ruled every shore of the Mediterranean, from the Atlantic to the Euphrates and from Hadrian's Wall to the first cataract of the Nile. Rome invented little that was wholly new and perfected almost everything it borrowed: Greek architecture became concrete vaults, Etruscan drains became aqueducts, and a city-state's customs became a body of law that most of Europe still lives under. Its language, Latin, is the parent of Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: Roman concrete, opus caementicium, mixed with volcanic ash so that it set even under water. The harbour moles built with it at Caesarea and Portus still stand.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: Vitruvius completes De architectura, ten books on building, water, machines and city planning that guided Renaissance architects fifteen centuries later.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: The Colosseum opens: about 50,000 seats, a retractable awning, and eighty entrances so the whole crowd could leave in minutes.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: The Pantheon's concrete dome, 43.3 meters across, is completed under Hadrian. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Pliny the Elder publishes the Natural History, thirty-seven books that try to gather everything then known about the natural world.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, writes the Almagest, the geocentric model of the heavens that stood for 1,400 years, and a Geography that placed the known world on a grid of coordinates.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Galen arrives in Rome. His dissections of animals describe the nerves, the heart and the pulse, and his anatomy is taught in Europe until the sixteenth century.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Aqueducts: eleven serve the city of Rome by 226 CE, feeding public fountains, baths and a sewer system, the Cloaca Maxima, that still drains the Forum.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Roads: about 80,000 km of paved highway across the empire by the second century, cambered for drainage, with milestones and way stations a day's ride apart.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The codex, pages bound at the spine, begins to replace the scroll; by the fourth century it is the normal form of the book.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The mills at Barbegal near Arles: sixteen water wheels in two descending rows, grinding grain for a whole town.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Virgil dies leaving the Aeneid unfinished. Augustus orders it published against the poet's wishes, and it becomes Rome's national epic.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ovid completes the Metamorphoses, the retelling of Greek and Roman myth that fed European painting and poetry for two thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Trajan's Column: a 30-meter spiral of carved relief telling the story of the Dacian wars in 155 scenes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Portrait sculpture that shows the sitter warts and all, mosaic floors from Britain to Syria, and the wall paintings of Pompeii, sealed by Vesuvius in 79 CE.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Roman law: the praetors' edicts and the jurists' commentaries, later gathered under Justinian, are the root of the civil law systems of continental Europe and Latin America.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Seneca, Stoic philosopher and tutor to Nero, is ordered to kill himself, leaving the Letters to Lucilius. Stoicism was the working philosophy of the Roman elite.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Constantine's Edict of Milan grants freedom of worship. Christianity, persecuted a decade earlier, becomes the religion of the emperors.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state religion.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Public baths in every town, with hot and cold rooms, exercise yards and libraries. Entry cost a quadrans, the smallest coin.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: A market the size of the Mediterranean: Spanish olive oil, Egyptian grain, Gaulish wine and Indian pepper moved in amphorae. Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill made of an estimated 53 million broken oil jars.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Insulae, apartment blocks of five or more storeys, housed most of Rome's roughly one million people, the largest city in the world until the nineteenth century.

On the death of Theodosius I in 395 the empire was divided between his sons Arcadius and Honorius and never reunited. The Western half fell in 476; the Eastern half, which we call Byzantine, lasted until 1453.

passages.text: The Safavids, who took Tabriz in 1501, made Twelver Shia Islam the religion of Iran and gave the country the shape and identity it has kept since. Shah Abbas I's Isfahan, the carpets, the painted manuscripts and the long wars with the Ottomans mark their two centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Shah Abbas I made Isfahan his capital and laid out the Naqsh-e Jahan square with the Shah Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah mosque and the Ali Qapu palace.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Ardabil carpet of 1539 to 1540 and the court workshops set the standard for Persian carpets, which reached European palaces by the thousands.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Reza Abbasi and the Isfahan painters, and the Shahnameh made for Shah Tahmasp with its 258 miniatures.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ismail I proclaimed Twelver Shia Islam the state religion at Tabriz and brought Shia scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A clerical hierarchy, the shrines of Mashhad and Qom and the mourning rites of Muharram took root.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Armenian Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians lived as protected communities, with periods of pressure.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Shah Abbas moved Armenian merchants from Julfa to New Julfa in Isfahan; their network carried Iranian silk to Venice, Amsterdam and India.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Isfahan grew into one of the largest cities of the seventeenth century, with its bazaar, bridges and gardens.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Twelver Shia Islam remains Iran's state religion.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Naqsh-e Jahan square was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Carpets and miniature painting remain the arts Iran is known for.
Afghan rebels took Isfahan in 1722 after a siege. Nader, an Afshar Turkmen general, drove them out, ruled through puppet Safavid shahs, and took the crown himself as Nader Shah in 1736.

passages.text: The Samanids, a Persian dynasty ruling from Bukhara from 819 to 999, presided over the revival of Persian as a written language after two centuries of Arabic. Their court fed the poets and scholars of the Islamic Golden Age in Central Asia.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Avicenna was born near Bukhara; his Canon of Medicine remained a standard medical text in Europe and the Islamic world into the seventeenth century.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Al-Biruni was born in Khwarazm and began his work in astronomy and mathematics as the Samanid age ended.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rudaki, called the father of Persian poetry, wrote at the court of Nasr II.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh, the Persian epic, under Samanid rule; he finished it in 1010.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bowls and plates from Nishapur and Samarkand carry black Kufic proverbs on white slip.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Persian became a language of court and literature beside Arabic; the vizier Bal'ami's Persian version of Tabari's history was made for the amir.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The dynasty was Sunni and patronized Hanafi scholars, and Bukhara became a center of Islamic learning.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Bukhara and Samarkand were the Silk Road's markets between China and the Islamic west.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Samanid silver dirhams were carried north along the Volga in such numbers that hoards of them turn up across Russia and Scandinavia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Persian literary revival shaped the Ghaznavid, Seljuk and later courts.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The mausoleum of the Samanids in Bukhara, a cube of patterned brick, is among the oldest surviving Islamic monuments in Central Asia.
The Karakhanids took Bukhara in 999 while the Ghaznavids, once Samanid slave-governors, took Khurasan south of the Oxus.

passages.text: The Great Seljuk Empire, founded when Tughril took Nishapur in 1037, brought Oghuz Turkic rule to Iran, Iraq and Anatolia under a Persian administration. Its sultans protected the Abbasid caliphs, built madrasas and mosques, and opened Anatolia to the Turks.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The vizier Nizam al-Mulk and his rival Taj al-Mulk added the two great brick domes to the Friday Mosque of Isfahan in 1086 and 1088.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Persian poetry, calligraphy and lustre ceramics flourished under Seljuk patronage; Omar Khayyam wrote the quatrains later gathered as the Rubaiyat.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, first of a network of madrasas teaching Shafi'i law and theology.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Alp Arslan's victory over the Byzantines at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Nizam al-Mulk's Book of Government set out the Persian art of kingship for the sultans.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Jalali calendar, computed by Omar Khayyam and colleagues for Malik Shah, fixed the year to the spring equinox with an error of about one day in 3,770 years, less than the Gregorian calendar's.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Khayyam's treatise on algebra classified cubic equations and solved them with conic sections.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Turkic settlement of Anatolia that followed Manzikert led to the Sultanate of Rum and, in time, the Ottomans.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The madrasa became the standard school of Sunni learning.

After Malik Shah's death in 1092 the empire split among his heirs and their atabegs. The last sultan of Iraq, Tughril III, was killed in 1194 by the Khwarazmshah Tekish, who took Iran; the Seljuks of Rum in Anatolia lasted until 1308.

passages.text: The Shang is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by contemporary written records, surviving on oracle bones and bronze inscriptions. Centered in the Anyang region, it controlled a network of towns and dependent settlements through ritual authority and bronze technology.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Oracle bone script, the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, carved on turtle plastrons and cattle shoulder blades to record the king's divinations. The earliest inscriptions date from the reign of Wu Ding.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Horse-drawn chariots appear in Shang burials at Anyang, adopted from the steppe, and are used for hunting, display and war.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Piece-mold bronze casting reaches its peak. The Houmuwu ding from Anyang, the heaviest bronze vessel known from the ancient world, weighs 832 kg.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A ten-day week and the sixty-day cycle of ten stems and twelve branches, still used in the Chinese calendar, organized Shang time; oracle bones are dated by the cycle.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Taotie masks and dragon motifs on bronze vessels show sophisticated design principles.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Jade carvings, marble sculptures and pottery figurines from royal tombs; the undisturbed tomb of Fu Hao, a consort of Wu Ding, held 755 jades and 468 bronzes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Musical instruments including bronze bells and stone chimes found in Anyang excavations.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The supreme deity Di ruled over lesser spirits and royal ancestors who mediated between heaven and earth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Royal divination addressed questions of war, harvest, weather, illness and the king's activities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Human sacrifice accompanied royal burials, with dozens or hundreds of victims in major tombs.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Millet farming, with rice and wheat as lesser crops, supported urban populations at Anyang and other centers.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Silk production, evident from the impressions of silk wrappings preserved on bronze vessels.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The king hunted from chariots with bows and bronze-tipped arrows.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cowrie shells from the Indian Ocean, given by the king as rewards and buried with the dead as wealth.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tin and copper for bronze imported from distant sources.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chinese writing system preserved in continuous use to the present day.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Bronze ritual vessel forms influenced Chinese metalwork for two thousand years.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The concept of a central royal authority over subordinate territories took root.
King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye, ending the dynasty.

passages.text: Shu Han claimed legitimacy as the true successor to the Han dynasty, ruling Sichuan under Liu Bei and his famous chancellor Zhuge Liang. Though the smallest of the Three Kingdoms, it became the most romanticized in later literature.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The repeating crossbow, known since the Warring States, was improved under Zhuge Liang by tradition, along with the wooden ox, a wheelbarrow-like cart for carrying supplies over mountain roads.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Sichuan's irrigation, built around the Dujiangyan works of the third century BCE, was kept up and extended to feed the state.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian legitimacy theory justified resistance to Cao Wei.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Loyalty and righteousness became central virtues in Shu Han ideology.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zhuge Liang became the archetype of the brilliant but tragic loyal minister in Chinese culture.
Cao Wei general Deng Ai led a surprise attack through mountain passes and captured Chengdu, forcing Liu Shan to surrender.

passages.text: Silla began as the smallest of Korea's Three Kingdoms, in the southeast around Gyeongju, and by 676 had brought most of the peninsula under one rule. Its bone-rank aristocracy, gold crowns, Hwarang youth bands and Buddhist temples made a distinctive civilization that lasted nearly a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gold crowns with tree and antler uprights, hung with jade and gold spangles, from the royal mound tombs of Gyeongju.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, with its granite Buddha facing the sea, were begun; UNESCO listed both in 1995.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cheomseongdae, a stone tower built in the reign of Queen Seondeok (632 to 647), is among the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in the world.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The bone-rank system fixed a person's rank, office and even the size of their house by birth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Hwarang, bands of aristocratic youths, trained in arms, song and Buddhist and Confucian teaching, and led Silla's armies.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism became the state religion after the martyrdom of Ichadon, and temples rose across the kingdom.

passages.title: Daily life

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Court culture prized refinement, poetry in the hyangga form and Buddhist devotion.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Gyeongju Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.text: The Song dynasty oversaw an economic and technological revolution in China, though military weakness led to the loss of northern China in 1127. Printing, gunpowder, the compass and paper money transformed society, while Neo-Confucianism shaped intellectual life.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Bi Sheng invents movable type printing, though woodblock remained more common.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The first gunpowder formulas for military use appear in the Wujing Zongyao military manual.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Shen Kuo describes the magnetic compass for navigation in his Dream Pool Essays.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Paper money, the jiaozi, issued by the government to facilitate commerce, the first state paper currency.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Early-ripening Champa rice from Vietnam is distributed to farmers, allowing two harvests a year in the south.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Landscape painting reaches its peak with masters like Fan Kuan and Guo Xi.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Porcelain production perfects celadon and qingbai wares.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zhu Xi (1130 to 1200) synthesizes Neo-Confucianism; his commentaries on the Four Books, completed about 1190, became the examination curriculum for six centuries.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Maritime trade with Southeast Asia, India and the Middle East expands dramatically.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Porcelain exported throughout Asia and eventually to the Middle East and Africa.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Song technological innovations transformed the world when transmitted to Europe.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Neo-Confucianism became the dominant ideology in East Asia until the nineteenth century.
The Mongol conquest was completed when the last Song emperor drowned at the fall of the final Song stronghold at Yamen in 1279; Kublai Khan ruled China as the Yuan dynasty.

passages.text: Srivijaya, a Malay kingdom based at Palembang on Sumatra from the seventh century, controlled the Strait of Malacca and the trade between India and China. Its rulers were patrons of Buddhism, and Old Malay, the language of its inscriptions, became the lingua franca of the archipelago.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The kingdom taxed ships passing the strait and made its ports the entrepot of the sea route between India and China.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Camphor, resins, gold, tin and spices went out; Chinese and Indian goods came in.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Missions to the Tang and Song courts kept the China trade open, and Arab writers knew the maharaja of Zabaj as lord of the islands.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Chinese monk Yijing stopped at Srivijaya in 671 and found more than a thousand monks; he advised pilgrims to study Sanskrit there before going on to India.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Kedukan Bukit inscription of 683, in Old Malay, is the oldest dated text in the language.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mahayana Buddhism had royal patronage; the scholar Atisha studied at Srivijaya for twelve years before carrying its teaching to Tibet.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malay spread as the trading language of the region and is the root of modern Malay and Indonesian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The pattern of a port kingdom ruling the strait passed to Malacca.
The Cholas sacked the ports in 1025, Malayu at Jambi took the lead, and Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit pressed on Sumatra; Majapahit's attack on Palembang in 1377 ended the old kingdom.

passages.text: The Sui dynasty reunited China after three centuries of division, creating institutions that the Tang would inherit and perfect. Its ambitious building projects and military campaigns exhausted the state, leading to its rapid collapse.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Grand Canal's main sections are dug between 605 and 610, connecting the Yellow River and Yangzi River systems for grain transport.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Standardization of coinage, weights and measures across the reunified empire.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism receives imperial patronage; Emperor Wen styled himself a Buddhist universal monarch.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations begin, recruiting officials by Confucian learning; the jinshi degree dates from about 605.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Grand Canal remained China's main north-south transport artery for over a thousand years.
Emperor Yang's disastrous Korean campaigns and excessive building projects led to widespread rebellion; he was assassinated by his own guards in 618.

passages.text: Sukhothai, which broke from Khmer rule about 1238, is remembered as the first Thai kingdom. Its inscription of Ram Khamhaeng describes a father-king, its sculptors made the walking Buddha, and its script became the Thai alphabet.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Ram Khamhaeng inscription, dated 1283, says the king devised the Thai script from Khmer models; some scholars date the stone itself to the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The walking Buddha, a figure in motion cast in bronze, is Sukhothai's own creation.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Lotus-bud chedis at Wat Mahathat and Sri Lankan-style bell stupas; glazed Sawankhalok stoneware was exported across the region.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism of the Sri Lankan school, brought by monks from Nakhon Si Thammarat, became the state religion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The inscription describes a king who hears any subject's grievance when they ring the bell at the palace gate.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic Town of Sukhothai and Associated Historic Towns were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Thai alphabet descends from the Sukhothai script.
Ayutthaya reduced Sukhothai to a vassal in 1378 and, when its royal line ended in 1438, made it a province.

passages.text: Drottningholm's eighteenth-century theatre used machinery that could change scenery while the curtain stayed up. Stage sets and working mechanisms survive.

passages.title: Trade and exchange

passages.text: The Tang dynasty is considered China's golden age, marked by cosmopolitan culture, Buddhist flourishing, poetic achievement and international trade. Chang'an became one of the world's largest cities, connected by the Silk Road to Central Asia, India and Persia.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Diamond Sutra, the world's oldest dated printed book, produced using woodblock printing.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The first written warning of gunpowder's power appears in a Daoist alchemical text, describing a mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal that burst into flame.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The great poets Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Wei create masterpieces of Chinese verse.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist cave temples at Dunhuang filled with murals and sculptures.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: True porcelain, the white Xing wares of Hebei, is made, though it remained rare and precious.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Xuanzang travels to India, returning in 645 with Buddhist texts that he translates.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Christianity arrives in Chang'an with the missionary Alopen; the Xi'an Stele of 781 records its reception.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Chang'an reaches a population of about one million, with foreign merchants, monks and diplomats.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Tea drinking becomes widespread; Lu Yu writes the Classic of Tea.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Silk Road trade connects China to Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Tang poetry became the standard for later Chinese literature.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Overseas Chinese still call a Chinatown a Tangrenjie, the street of the Tang people.
The An Lushan Rebellion of 755 fatally weakened the dynasty; regional military governors gained power, and the last Tang emperor was deposed by Zhu Wen in 907.

passages.text: Teotihuacan was a major urban center in central Mexico. Its public monuments, apartment compounds and specialized arts connected a large city with other Mesoamerican communities through exchange and influence.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The urban layout incorporated the San Juan River, whose course was altered to cross the Avenue of the Dead.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Builders used talud-tablero profiles, combining sloping and upright wall sections, in civil and religious architecture.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Apartment compounds grouped connected rooms around open courtyards. They provided durable shared housing for much of the city's population.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Murals decorated many buildings, especially residential compounds. Artists also made mold-pressed ceramics and geometric stone faces.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imported craft goods included worked obsidian and Thin Orange pottery. Stackable bowls made long-distance transport more practical.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The Met's updated account places burning in the monumental core around 550 CE and marked population decline after 600. The people responsible are unidentified.

passages.text: The Tibetan Empire rose under Songtsen Gampo in the seventh century and for two hundred years matched Tang China and the Arab caliphate for control of the Silk Road, from the Tarim Basin to the Himalaya. It gave Tibet its script, its first monasteries and its Buddhism.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Songtsen Gampo married Princess Wencheng of Tang, who brought a Buddha image and texts to Lhasa; a Nepalese princess, Bhrikuti, is remembered as his other Buddhist queen.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Tibetan script was created, by tradition by Thonmi Sambhota, from an Indian script of the Gupta type.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Samye, the first Tibetan Buddhist monastery, was completed under Trisong Detsen, and Buddhism spread beside the native Bon rites.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Jokhang temple was built in Lhasa and became Tibet's holiest shrine.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tibetan armies fielded armored cavalry and took fortified towns with methods learned from China and Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tibet held the Tarim oases and, from 786 to 848, Dunhuang, taxing the Silk Road between China, India and Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: A Tibetan army occupied the Tang capital Chang'an for about two weeks.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: A peace treaty with Tang was carved in Tibetan and Chinese on a pillar that still stands outside the Jokhang.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Tibetan script is in use today across Tibet, Bhutan and the Himalaya.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Buddhism became the core of Tibetan identity and culture.
The emperor Langdarma was assassinated in 842 and the empire broke into rival kingdoms, the Era of Fragmentation, that lasted until the eleventh century.

passages.title: Arts

passages.text: Vijayanagara, founded on the Tungabhadra in 1336, ruled the south of India for three centuries and made its capital, today's Hampi, one of the largest cities in the world. It kept the temple culture of the Tamil and Kannada country alive and traded horses and spices with the Portuguese, the Arabs and China.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gopurams, towered gateways, and pillared halls carried Dravidian temple building to its most elaborate.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Under Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 1529) the Krishna temple was built at Hampi and the Vittala temple gained its stone chariot and musical pillars.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Krishnadevaraya kept eight Telugu poets at court and wrote the Amuktamalyada himself; Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit letters flourished too.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Arab and Portuguese traders sold the warhorses the empire needed; Hampi's markets sold diamonds, spices and cloth.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Portuguese Domingo Paes, who saw the city about 1520, called it as large as Rome and the best provided city in the world.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Estimates of the capital's people run to several hundred thousand, among the largest cities of the sixteenth century.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Canals from the Tungabhadra and large tanks watered the fields around the city.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Group of Monuments at Hampi was listed by UNESCO; more than 1,600 remains survive.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The empire's temple styles and its Nayaka successors kept Hindu kingship alive in the south.

The Deccan sultanates crushed the imperial army at Talikota in 1565 and sacked the capital. The Aravidu kings ruled a shrinking realm from Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore until Bijapur and Golconda took the last of it in 1646.

passages.text: Wessex was a kingdom in southern England. Under Alfred, royal support for reading and translation linked learned texts with the skilled production of books and precious objects.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Alfred commissioned translations of religious works from Latin into Old English. Copies circulated within his kingdom.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Some books were accompanied by reading pointers called aestels. The Alfred Jewel may have formed the head of one, but its function remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The jewel combines gold, colored cloisonne enamel and rock crystal. A figure appears beneath the crystal, and an animal-like head forms the base.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: An inscription names Alfred as the person who ordered the object made. The museum dates it to his reign, 871 to 899.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The figure beneath the crystal may personify sight, fitting a possible reading aid. The museum presents this identification as uncertain.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: Alfred's law code drew on earlier West Saxon, Mercian and Kentish rules. His government also supported fortified market settlements, connecting defense with economic activity.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Wessex became the base from which Alfred's successors expanded royal power across England. This was a process of political consolidation, not the disappearance of West Saxon people.
