passages.text: The Western Zhou established the political and philosophical foundations of Chinese civilization. Through a system of enfeoffment and the concept of the Mandate of Heaven, they created a model of legitimate rulership that endured for three millennia.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Mandate of Heaven concept emerges, stating that Heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Duke of Zhou articulates the theory of dynastic succession and the ruler's moral responsibility.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ancestor worship becomes formalized in ritual bronze vessels and temple ceremonies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The first smelted iron in China, blades set in bronze handles, appears at the very end of the period; iron remained rare beside bronze.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Improved bronze casting techniques for ritual vessels, bells and weapons; the yongzhong bell, hung at an angle and struck at two points, takes its form.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The songs of the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), court hymns and folk songs, date from this period; the anthology was assembled later.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The core of the Book of Changes (Yijing), the hexagram and line statements, takes shape as a divination manual; the philosophical commentaries came centuries later.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze inscriptions become longer and more literary, recording royal deeds and land grants; the Mao Gong ding carries about 500 characters.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Regional lords governed territories from walled cities, owing military service and tribute to the Zhou king.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The well-field system supposedly divided agricultural land into nine plots, with the center plot worked for the lord.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Confucius later idealized the Western Zhou as a golden age of virtue and proper ritual.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Mandate of Heaven justified political change throughout Chinese history until the empire ended in 1912.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zhou ritual codes influenced East Asian court ceremonies for centuries.
Quanrong nomads allied with disaffected lords sacked the capital Haojing and killed King You, forcing the court to flee east.

passages.text: The Xia is the first dynasty in Chinese tradition, associated by most Chinese scholars with the Erlitou archaeological culture of the middle Yellow River valley. Whether it was a historical state or a later political myth remains debated outside China, but the material culture of the period shows the first large-scale bronze production and palace architecture in the region.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Erlitou casts the earliest Chinese bronze ritual vessels, small jue wine cups, in sectioned clay moulds, the piece-mould method the Shang would carry to its height.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Flood control and irrigation works are attributed by tradition to the founder Yu the Great; the story is legend, but the Yellow River floodplain was being farmed and managed in this period.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Plain bronze jue and jade blades, sceptres and cong tubes from Erlitou set the forms that later dynasties elaborated and decorated.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Turquoise-inlaid bronze plaques with animal designs, and a dragon of some two thousand turquoise pieces laid on a body in an Erlitou tomb.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ancestor offerings and divination with burnt animal bones appear in the archaeological record, anticipating Shang and Zhou religion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The legend of Yu controlling the floods established the model of the virtuous ruler who brings order from chaos.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Millet farming and pig husbandry supported growing populations in the Yellow River valley.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Rammed-earth foundations and walls enclosed the palace compound at Erlitou, a walled precinct of about eleven hectares.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: In the traditional histories the cycle of dynasties begins with the Xia: Tang of Shang overthrows its last king, and the Zhou later name the pattern the Mandate of Heaven.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Xia later became synonymous with Chinese civilization itself, in the word Huaxia.
According to tradition, the tyrant Jie was defeated by Tang of Shang at the Battle of Mingtiao.

passages.text: The Xin dynasty was a brief interregnum when Wang Mang attempted radical reforms inspired by ancient Zhou ideals. His policies failed to address real economic problems and natural disasters, above all the Yellow River's change of course, and ended in widespread rebellion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Wang Mang claims the Mandate of Heaven has transferred to him based on omens and classical precedents.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Reforms modeled on the ancient Zhou well-field system and ritual codes.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Private land ownership abolished; all land declared the king's fields, to be redistributed in equal shares. The order was withdrawn within three years.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The trade in slaves banned, though the ban was widely ignored.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: State monopolies on salt, iron, coinage and liquor, and a bureau to lend to farmers and steady prices.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Wang Mang's failure discredited radical reform and strengthened conservative Confucianism.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: His reign became a cautionary tale about ignoring economic realities for ideological purity.
Rebel armies captured Chang'an in 23 CE and killed Wang Mang; a Han prince, Liu Xiu, restored the dynasty in 25 as Emperor Guangwu.

passages.text: The Xiongnu were the first great steppe empire, united by Modu Chanyu in 209 BCE and ruling Mongolia and the lands to its west for three centuries. Their mounted archers, tribute treaties with Han China and left-and-right administration set the pattern for the Turkic and Mongol empires that followed.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Composite bows of horn and sinew, shot from the saddle, made every herdsman a warrior.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Bronze and iron for weapons and harness; gold plaques of animals in combat for the elite.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The chanyu ruled under Heaven, Tengri, with shamans and seasonal gatherings to sacrifice to ancestors, heaven and earth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Elite tombs at Noin-Ula held Chinese silks, lacquer and Bactrian textiles beside the dead.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The heqin treaties from 198 BCE brought Han princesses, silk, grain and wine to the chanyu as the price of peace.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Xiongnu taxed the oasis towns of the Tarim Basin and traded horses and furs to China.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Xiongnu model of steppe empire was followed by the Turkic khaganates and the Mongols.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Their name may lie behind the Huns of European sources, though the link is unproven.

The confederation split into southern and northern halves in 54 BCE. Han armies broke the Northern Xiongnu at Ikh Bayan in 89 CE, and by 93 the Xianbei had taken over the steppe; the Southern Xiongnu lived on as Han clients inside the Great Wall.

passages.text: The Yamato period covers the rise of a single Japanese state from the chiefdoms of the Kofun age. Great keyhole-shaped tombs mark the power of the early rulers; in the sixth and seventh centuries the court took Buddhism, writing and Chinese-style government from Korea and China.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Keyhole-shaped kofun mounds for rulers; the largest, the Daisen Kofun near Osaka, is 486 meters long.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Haniwa clay figures of warriors, horses, houses and dancers stood on the mounds.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze mirrors, iron swords and gilt-bronze horse trappings came from Korea and China and were buried with the chiefs.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism arrived from Baekje, and the Soga and Mononobe clans fought over whether to accept it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Prince Shotoku's Seventeen-Article Constitution set out Buddhist and Confucian principles for officials.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Native kami worship, later called Shinto, continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron tools and weapons improved through smiths and ore from the Korean kingdoms.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Chinese writing was adopted for court records; the inscribed sword from Inariyama, dated to 471, is among the earliest texts written in Japan.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Taika Reform began to remodel the court and its land system on Tang lines.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The imperial line that emerged in this period continues to the present.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group was listed by UNESCO.
The court moved to a permanent capital at Heijo-kyo in 710, the start of the Nara period.

passages.text: Yolngu peoples maintain distinct clan identities in Arnhem Land. Country, law, food, ceremony and art remain connected, while institutions at Yirrkala carry knowledge through contemporary media.

passages.title: Worldview and institutions
passages.text: Dhuwa and Yirritja are complementary moieties connecting people, places and other living beings. In Miwatj, art and ceremony express relationships to fresh and saltwater Country.

passages.title: Food and seasons
passages.text: Seasonal food gathering draws on both land and sea, including yams, fruit, fish and shellfish. Traditional owners connect these practices with law and ceremony.

passages.title: Art and diplomacy
passages.text: Artists framed the Yirrkala petitions with clan designs in ochre, charcoal and pipeclay. These designs expressed relationships to land alongside text in English and Yolngu Matha.

passages.title: Political history
passages.text: Yolngu presented bark petitions to the Australian Parliament in 1963 in response to mining plans made without adequate consultation. They understood the documents as a diplomatic offering between equal powers.

passages.title: Digital knowledge
passages.text: The Mulka Project combines a recording studio, production house, learning centre and cultural archive under Yolngu law and elder leadership. It trains community members and returns audiovisual records to communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A bark petition formerly held privately was formally returned to Yolngu at Yirrkala in 2023. Its return forms part of continuing cultural custody.

passages.text: Monte Alban was an important Zapotec capital in the Oaxaca Valley. Its history of urban planning, water management and carved inscriptions is one part of the much wider history of Zapotec societies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders reshaped hillsides with terraces, dams and conduits. Water management and the creation of level spaces were integrated into urban development.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Temples and platforms framed a long ceremonial esplanade. Open spaces were as important to the layout as the buildings themselves.

passages.title: Writing and arts
passages.text: Carved reliefs with hieroglyphic inscriptions survive alongside tombs and temples, giving evidence of visual art and record making.

passages.title: Public life
passages.text: The ceremonial center included a ball court. Its built spaces supported activities beyond the palaces and burial places of elites.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Monte Alban maintained relations with Teotihuacan. Those contacts connect Oaxaca's history to other contemporary Mesoamerican centers.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: UNESCO dates Monte Alban's long florescence from about 500 BCE to 850 CE, followed by decline. This is the trajectory of a city, not an extinction date for Zapotec peoples.
